<!-- maintheorem-1: body_md -->
\label{amp:main}
Let $X$ be a compact connected complex manifold of positive dimension.
If $X$ is Brody hyperbolic and admits a smooth plurinegative Hermitian
metric, then $X$ is projective and $K_X$ is ample.
<!-- end maintheorem-1 -->
<!-- maincorollary-1: body_md -->
\label{amp:cor:negative}
Let $(X,h)$ be a compact Hermitian manifold with strictly negative
Chern HSC. If $X$ admits a smooth plurinegative Hermitian metric,
then $X$ is projective and $K_X$ is ample.
<!-- end maincorollary-1 -->
<!-- maintheorem-2: body_md -->
\label{n:thm:main}
Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $n\ge2$ in Fujiki's
class $\mathcal C$, and let $h$ be a smooth Hermitian metric with
$H_h\equiv c\le0$. Then $h$ is K\"ahler. More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $c<0$, then $X$ is projective and $K_X$ is ample. With
$\lambda_c=(n+1)c/2$, $h$ is the unique K\"ahler--Einstein metric satisfying
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_h^{(1)}=\lambda_c\omega_h,\qquad
[\omega_h]=\frac{2\pi}{-\lambda_c}c_1(K_X).
\]
Its universal cover is complex hyperbolic space of holomorphic sectional
curvature $c$.
\item If $c=0$, then $h$ is flat K\"ahler. Its universal cover is
Euclidean, and a finite \'etale cover of $X$ is a complex torus on which
the lifted metric is translation invariant.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end maintheorem-2 -->
<!-- maintheorem-3: body_md -->
\label{p:thm:main}\label{p:cor:cp}\label{z:thm:threefold}
Let $X$ be a compact complex threefold, and let $h$ be a smooth
Hermitian metric with constant Chern HSC $c$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $c\ne0$, then $h$ is K\"ahler. For $c>0$, $(X,h)$ is
holomorphically isometric to $\mathbb P^3$ with a scaled Fubini--Study metric;
for $c<0$, its universal cover is complex hyperbolic three-space.
In both cases the holomorphic sectional curvature is $c$.
\item If $c=0$, then the original metric is Chern flat: $R^h=0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end maintheorem-3 -->
<!-- maintheorem-4: body_md -->
\label{ce:thm:main}\label{ce:thm:allhigher}
For every integer $n\ge7$ there is a compact connected Hermitian
manifold $(X_n,h_n)$ of complex dimension $n$ such that
\[
H_{h_n}\equiv0,\qquad R^{h_n}\not\equiv0,\qquad
d\omega_{h_n}^{n-1}=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Ric}_{h_n}^{(j)}=0\quad(1\le j\le4).
\]
Moreover, $K_{X_n}$ admits a nowhere-zero Chern-parallel holomorphic
volume form.
<!-- end maintheorem-4 -->
<!-- maintheorem-5: body_md -->
\label{ext:thm:auxiliary}
Let $(X^n,h)$ be a compact Hermitian manifold with
$H_h\equiv0$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_h^{(1)}=0$. Suppose that $X$ admits a smooth
semipositive real $(1,1)$-form $\kappa$ which is positive definite at
some point and satisfies $i\partial\bar\partial\kappa\le0$ on
decomposable complex two-vectors. Then $h$ is flat K\"ahler.
Its universal cover is holomorphically isometric to $\mathbb C^n$, and
$X$ has a finite \'etale cover by a complex torus.
<!-- end maintheorem-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{univ:analyticity}\label{lemma:analyticity}\label{c0:r1:analytic}
A smooth Hermitian metric with constant Chern holomorphic sectional
curvature, in any complex dimension and for any real constant $c$,
is real analytic in holomorphic coordinates.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\label{app:analyticity-calculation}
In fixed holomorphic coordinates set
$\mathcal Q_{i\bar j k\bar l}
=h^{a\bar b}(\partial_i h_{k\bar b})(\partial_{\bar j}h_{a\bar l})$.
Contracting the four-slot polarization with the fixed coordinate matrix
$\delta^{k\bar l}$ gives $\mathscr A h=\mathscr N(h,Dh)$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:global-operator}
 \begin{split}
 (\mathscr A u)_{i\bar j}=-\bigl(&
 \sum_k\partial_k\partial_{\bar k}u_{i\bar j}
 +\partial_i\partial_{\bar j}\operatorname{tr} u+\sum_k\partial_k\partial_{\bar j}u_{i\bar k}
 +\sum_k\partial_i\partial_{\bar k}u_{k\bar j}\bigr).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathscr N_{i\bar j}
 ={}&2c\sum_k(h_{i\bar j}h_{k\bar k}+h_{i\bar k}h_{k\bar j})-\sum_k(\mathcal Q_{i\bar j k\bar k}+\mathcal Q_{k\bar j i\bar k}
 +\mathcal Q_{i\bar k k\bar j}+\mathcal Q_{k\bar k i\bar j}).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Choose a fixed real orthonormal basis of the Hermitian matrices, so
that $h$ has $n^2$ real component functions on a domain in $\mathbb R^{2n}$.
The operator $\mathscr A$ has constant coefficients: the contraction
above uses the fixed matrix $\delta^{k\bar l}$, not $h^{k\bar l}$.
The map $\mathscr N(h,Dh)$ is real analytic on the positive Hermitian
cone, because matrix inversion is analytic there and the remaining
operations are polynomial.
Left-multiply the system by
$\mathcal S_0(v)=v+(\operatorname{tr} v)I$. This is an invertible real-linear map,
with inverse $\mathcal S_0^{-1}(v)=v-(\operatorname{tr} v)I/(n+1)$, so the new
system is equivalent to the original one.
Write $z^j=x^j+iy^j$, so
$\partial_j=(\partial_{x^j}-i\partial_{y^j})/2$, and use the real
principal symbol obtained by replacing each $\partial_{x^j}$ and
$\partial_{y^j}$ by $i\xi_{x^j}$ and $i\xi_{y^j}$.
By unitary invariance, it suffices to check the unit real covector
$\xi_0=dx^0$. For
$u=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x&z^*\\z&W\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and
$t=\operatorname{tr} W$, the exact symbol is
$\sigma(\mathscr A)(\xi_0)u
=\frac14\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4x+t&2z^*\\2z&W\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{hd-elliptic-square}
 \begin{split}
 4\langle u,\mathcal S_0\sigma(\mathscr A)(\xi_0)u\rangle
 &=8x^2+7xt+2t^2+4|z|^2+|W|^2\\
 &=x^2+\tfrac14t^2+7(x+t/2)^2+4|z|^2+|W|^2
 \ge |u|^2.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
By homogeneity, the real principal symbol satisfies the explicit bound
$\langle u,\mathcal S_0\sigma(\mathscr A)(\xi)u\rangle
\ge\frac14|\xi|^2|u|^2$ at every real covector. Thus the
linearization of
$\mathcal S_0\mathscr A h-\mathcal S_0\mathscr N(h,Dh)=0$
is a strongly elliptic system; its principal part is the same
constant-coefficient operator, since $\mathscr N$ contains only
zeroth and first derivatives.
On a sufficiently small closed coordinate ball, $h$ remains in the
positive cone and, being smooth, belongs to $C^{2,\mu}$ for every
$0<\mu<1$. These are the hypotheses of Morrey's interior theorem
for analytic nonlinear systems
\cite[\S6.7, Theorem~6.7.6, p.~271]{Morrey}.
In the notation of that section, take $N=n^2$, $s_j=0$, and $t_k=2$;
subtracting the degree-two Taylor polynomial at the chosen interior
point gives the normalization in (6.7.3)--(6.7.5).
Hence $h$ is real analytic near every point.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{n:lem:no-rational-kahler}
A compact complex manifold in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$ with no
rational curves is K\"ahler.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
A smooth complex manifold is strongly $\mathbb Q$-factorial, since
rank-one reflexive sheaves are line bundles. The trivial generalized
pair $(X,0)$ is generalized klt. Hacon--Li--Xie
\cite[Corollary~1.4]{HaconLiXie} show that such a class-$\mathcal C$
space is K\"ahler unless its curve-current cone contains a class
$-[C]$ with $C$ rational. The hypothesis excludes this alternative.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:pre:hyperbolic}
If $H_k\le-\kappa<0$, every entire holomorphic map $\mathbb C\to X$ is constant.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For a holomorphic curve $f$, put $e=|f'|_k^2$.
On the open set $e>0$, the Chern metric differentiation formula gives
\[
 \partial_z\partial_{\bar z}\log e
 =\frac{|\nabla_z f'|^2 e-|\langle\nabla_zf',f'\rangle|^2}{e^2}
       -\frac{R^k(f',\bar f',f',\bar f')}{e}
 \ge\kappa e.
\]
This formula follows by twice differentiating $\langle f',f'\rangle_k$ in
holomorphic coordinates and substituting the displayed curvature
formula; the first numerator is nonnegative by Cauchy--Schwarz.
On $|z|<R$, the function
\[
 b_R(z)=\frac{2R^2}{\kappa(R^2-|z|^2)^2}
\]
satisfies $\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}\log b_R=\kappa b_R$.
When $f$ is defined on a neighborhood of the closed radius-$R$ disc,
$e/b_R$ tends to zero at its boundary. If its maximum exceeded one,
it would occur with $e>0$, where the second derivative test applied to
$\log(e/b_R)$ contradicts $\kappa(e-b_R)>0$. Hence
$e(0)\le2/(\kappa R^2)$. For an entire curve, let $R\to\infty$ and
apply this at each source center. Its derivative vanishes everywhere.
This is the one-dimensional Hermitian Ahlfors--Schwarz argument;
no K\"ahler symmetry is used.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:pre:green}
For smooth $u$ on $\mathbb D$ and $r<1$,
\begin{align}
 \langle u\rangle_r-u(0)
 &=\frac2\pi\int_{|z|<r}\log\frac r{|z|}
       \partial_z\partial_{\bar z}u\,\mathrm d S,\label{amp:app:eq:green-poisson}\\
 \frac1\pi\int_{|z|<r}\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}u\,\mathrm d S
 &=\frac r2\langle\partial_r u\rangle_r.\label{amp:app:eq:green-area}
\end{align}
If $u\in C^0(\overline\mathbb D)$ and
$\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}u\in L^a(\mathbb D)$ for some $a>1$,
the first identity passes to $r=1$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
These are the planar Green formulas with
$\Delta=4\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}$. The passage to $r=1$ follows
from continuity of circle means and H\"older's inequality, since
$\log(1/|z|)$ belongs to every finite $L^b(\mathbb D)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:ex:brody}
There is a constant $D>0$, depending only on $(X,k)$, such that every
holomorphic map $f\colon\mathbb D\to X$ satisfies
\[
 d(f)=|f'(0)|_k^2\leq D.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 |f'(z)|_k\leq\frac{\sqrt D}{1-|z|},\qquad z\in\mathbb D.
 \label{amp:app:eq:brody-derivative}
\end{equation}
Every sequence of such maps has a subsequence converging uniformly on
compact subsets of $\mathbb D$ to a holomorphic map into $X$. In local target
coordinates, all derivatives converge uniformly on smaller compact
subsets as well.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We give Brody's rescaling argument in the normalization needed here
\cite{amp:old:Brody1978}.
Suppose first that there are maps $f_j\colon\mathbb D\to X$ with
$|f_j'(0)|_k\to\infty$. Choose $z_j$ at which the continuous function
\[
 z\longmapsto (1/2-|z|)|f_j'(z)|_k
\]
attains its maximum on $\{|z|\leq1/2\}$. For all sufficiently large $j$
this maximum is positive, so $|z_j|<1/2$. Put
\[
 \lambda_j=|f_j'(z_j)|_k,
 \qquad R_j=(1/2-|z_j|)\lambda_j,
 \qquad g_j(w)=f_j(z_j+w/\lambda_j).
\]
The map $g_j$ is defined on $\{|w|<R_j\}$, and
\[
 R_j\geq\tfrac12|f_j'(0)|_k\longrightarrow\infty,
 \qquad |g_j'(0)|_k=1.
\]
If $|w|<R_j/2$, then
\[
 1/2-|z_j+w/\lambda_j|
 \geq\tfrac12(1/2-|z_j|).
\]
The maximizing property of $z_j$ therefore gives
$|g_j'(w)|_k\leq2$ on this smaller disc.

For every fixed radius these maps are consequently equicontinuous and
take values in the compact metric space $X$. The Arzel\`a--Ascoli theorem
and a diagonal subsequence give a locally uniform limit
$g\colon\mathbb C\to X$. To verify holomorphy, choose a point of the source and
a target coordinate chart containing its image under $g$. On a
sufficiently small source neighborhood, the limit and all sufficiently
late maps take values in that chart. Their coordinate representations
converge uniformly on smaller neighborhoods. The usual theorem on
uniform limits of holomorphic functions, followed by the Cauchy
integral formula for derivatives, shows that $g$ is holomorphic and
$|g'(0)|_k=1$. This contradicts the hypothesis on entire maps. The
central derivative bound follows.

For $z\in\mathbb D$, apply this bound to
$w\mapsto f(z+(1-|z|)w)$. Its central derivative is
$(1-|z|)f'(z)$, proving Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:brody-derivative}. The estimate gives
equicontinuity on every compact source disc. A second application of
Arzel\`a--Ascoli and the same coordinate argument proves normality and
convergence of derivatives. Increasing $D$ if necessary makes it
strictly positive.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:ex:maximizer}
The functional in Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:disc-functional} has finite
supremum, attained by a finite-area holomorphic disc centered at $x$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Choose $C_q\geq0$ such that
\[
 |q(v,v)|\leq C_q \langle v,v\rangle_k
\]
for every tangent vector $v$. Select $r_0\in[1/2,1)$ so close to $1$
that $2C_q\log(1/r_0)\leq\delta/2$. For a disc $f$ write
\[
 a_f(z)=\langle f'(z),f'(z)\rangle_k,\qquad b_f(z)=q(f'(z),f'(z)).
\]
On the outer annulus $r_0<|z|<1$, the function
\[
 T_f(z)=\delta a_f(z)-2\log(1/|z|)b_f(z)
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 T_f(z)\geq\frac\delta2 a_f(z)\geq0.
 \label{amp:app:eq:negative-tail-density}
\end{equation}
On the inner disc, Lemma~\ref{amp:app:ex:brody} give a uniform bound for $a_f$ and $|b_f|$. Since
$\log(1/|z|)$ is integrable there, there is a constant $K$ independent
of $f$ such that
\[
 \left|\frac1\pi\int_{|z|<r_0}
 \bigl(2\log(1/|z|)b_f(z)-\delta a_f(z)\bigr)\,dS\right|
 \leq K.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 J_{k,q,\delta}(f)
 \leq D+K-\frac\delta{2\pi}\int_{r_0<|z|<1}a_f\,dS.
 \label{amp:app:eq:maximizing-area-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular, the supremum is finite. It is nonnegative because the
constant disc has value zero.

Choose a maximizing sequence $(f_j)$ with $J_{k,q,\delta}(f_j)\geq-1$.
Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:maximizing-area-bound} bounds its outer-annulus
areas uniformly, and the compact-interior derivative estimate bounds
its inner areas. Thus
\[
 \sup_j A_k(f_j)<\infty.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{amp:app:ex:brody}, after passing to a subsequence the maps converge
locally uniformly to a holomorphic disc $f$ centered at $x$. Derivative
convergence on compact subsets gives pointwise convergence of $a_{f_j}$
and $b_{f_j}$. Fatou's lemma gives
$A_k(f)\leq\liminf_j A_k(f_j)<\infty$.

We verify the required upper semicontinuity of $J$. Its central term
converges by derivative convergence. Its inner-disc integral converges
by dominated convergence, using the uniform bound above together with
the integrable logarithmic weight. On the outer annulus, the
nonnegative functions $T_{f_j}$ converge pointwise to $T_f$, so Fatou's
lemma yields
\[
 -\frac1\pi\int_{r_0<|z|<1}T_f\,dS
 \geq\limsup_j
 \left(-\frac1\pi\int_{r_0<|z|<1}T_{f_j}\,dS\right).
\]
All these integrals are finite. Indeed, finite area controls the
unweighted integrals and the logarithmic weight is bounded on the
outer annulus. Combining the three terms proves
\[
 J_{k,q,\delta}(f)\geq\limsup_jJ_{k,q,\delta}(f_j),
\]
which proves attainment.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:ex:dilation}
If $f$ is a maximizer in Proposition~\ref{amp:app:ex:maximizer}, then, for
$0<r<1$,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 0\leq\delta\bigl(A_k(f)-A_{k,r}(f)\bigr)
 &\leq(1-r^2)d(f)
       +2\int_r^1 A_{q,s}(f)\,\frac{ds}{s}.
 \end{split}
 \label{amp:app:eq:tail}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 A_q(f)\geq-d(f),\qquad
 A_k(f)-A_{k,r}(f)\leq C_f(1-r)\quad(1/2\leq r<1)
 \label{amp:app:eq:extremal-area-tail}
\end{equation}
for some finite constant $C_f$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $f_r(z)=f(rz)$. A change of variables gives
\[
 d(f_r)=r^2d(f),\qquad
 A_k(f_r)=A_{k,r}(f),\qquad
 A_{q,s}(f_r)=A_{q,rs}(f).
\]
The identity $\log(1/|z|)=\int_{|z|}^1ds/s$ and Fubini's theorem give
\[
 P_q(f)=2\int_0^1 A_{q,s}(f)\,\frac{ds}{s}.
\]
Fubini is valid also for this signed integrand: near the origin the
coordinate derivatives of $f$ are bounded, while away from the
origin the logarithmic weight is bounded and $|q(f',f')|$ is controlled
by the finite $k$-area. Applying the same identity to $f_r$ gives
\begin{equation}
 P_q(f)-P_q(f_r)
   =2\int_r^1 A_{q,s}(f)\,\frac{ds}{s}.
 \label{amp:app:eq:dilation-poisson}
\end{equation}
Since $f_r$ has the same center and finite area, maximality gives
$J_{k,q,\delta}(f)\geq J_{k,q,\delta}(f_r)$. Substituting the three
identities proves Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:tail}; its leftmost inequality uses the
positivity of $k$.

Divide the rightmost expression in Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:tail} by $1-r$. As
$r\uparrow1$, it tends to $2d(f)+2A_q(f)$. It is nonnegative for every
$r$, and hence $A_q(f)\geq-d(f)$. For $r\geq1/2$, the original
right-hand side of Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:tail} is at most
\[
 2d(f)(1-r)+4C_qA_k(f)(1-r).
\]
This bounds the $k$-area tail by a constant times $1-r$. This gives the second assertion in
Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:extremal-area-tail}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:ex:regularity}
Every disc maximizing the functional in Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:disc-functional}
extends continuously
to $\overline\mathbb D$ and belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb D,X)$ for every $2<p<4$.
In particular, it has continuous $W^{1,3}$ regularity up to the
boundary. More precisely, there is a constant $C_f$ such that
\begin{equation}
 |f'(z)|_k\leq C_f(1-|z|)^{-1/2}
 \label{amp:app:eq:boundary-derivative}
\end{equation}
for $z$ sufficiently close to $\partial\mathbb D$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We first make precise the uniform choice of target charts for small
source discs. Choose finitely many nested coordinate neighborhoods
\[
 V_\alpha\Subset W_\alpha\Subset U_\alpha
\]
such that the $V_\alpha$ cover $X$ and each $U_\alpha$ is a holomorphic
coordinate chart. By compactness, there is a number $\rho>0$ such that
if $y\in V_\alpha$, its metric ball of radius $\rho$ is contained in
$W_\alpha$. On each $\overline{W_\alpha}$, the metric $k$ and the
Euclidean coordinate metric are uniformly comparable; one comparison
constant suffices for this finite collection.

For $z\in\mathbb D$ put $t=1-|z|$. Let $0<c<1/4$, to be fixed independently
of $z$ and $f$. For $w\in B(z,ct)$, the straight segment from $z$ to
$w$ stays at source distance at least $(1-c)t$ from $\partial\mathbb D$.
Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:brody-derivative} therefore bounds the length of
its image by
\[
 C\sqrt D\,\frac{c}{1-c},
\]
where $C$ accounts only for the convention relating real and complex
tangent norms. Choose $c$ small enough that this bound is less than
$\rho$. Selecting $\alpha$ with $f(z)\in V_\alpha$, we obtain
\[
 f\bigl(B(z,ct)\bigr)\subset W_\alpha.
\]

In these coordinates the derivative of $f$ is a vector of holomorphic
functions. Its squared Euclidean norm is subharmonic. The mean-value
inequality and the uniform metric comparisons give
\[
 |f'(z)|_k^2
 \leq\frac{C_1}{t^2}
       \int_{B(z,ct)}|f'(w)|_k^2\,dS(w).
\]
Every point of $B(z,ct)$ has modulus greater than
$1-(1+c)t$. For $t$ sufficiently small, the area-tail estimate in
Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:extremal-area-tail} consequently gives
\[
 \int_{B(z,ct)}|f'(w)|_k^2\,dS(w)
 \leq\pi\bigl(A_k(f)-A_{k,1-(1+c)t}(f)\bigr)
 \leq C_2t.
\]
This proves Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:boundary-derivative}.

For $r<s<1$ sufficiently close to $1$ and $\zeta\in\partial\mathbb D$,
integration along the radial segment gives
\[
 \operatorname{dist}_k\bigl(f(r\zeta),f(s\zeta)\bigr)
 \leq C_3\int_r^s(1-u)^{-1/2}\,du
 \leq2C_3\sqrt{1-r}.
\]
The estimate is uniform in $\zeta$. Since $X$ is complete, each radial
path has a limit, and the continuous maps
$\zeta\mapsto f(r\zeta)$ converge uniformly as $r\uparrow1$. Their
limit is therefore continuous on $\partial\mathbb D$. The same uniform
estimate, together with continuity of this boundary map, proves that
the resulting extension of $f$ is continuous on all of $\overline\mathbb D$.

It remains to improve the integrability of the derivative. For all
sufficiently large integers $j$, let
\[
 E_j=\{z\in\mathbb D:2^{-j-1}<1-|z|<2^{-j}\}.
\]
The area-tail estimate and Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:boundary-derivative} imply
\[
 \int_{E_j}|f'|_k^2\,dS\leq C_4\,2^{-j},
 \qquad
 \sup_{E_j}|f'|_k\leq C_5\,2^{j/2}.
\]
Thus, for $2<p<4$,
\[
 \begin{split}
 \int_{E_j}|f'|_k^p\,dS
 &\leq\bigl(\sup_{E_j}|f'|_k\bigr)^{p-2}
              \int_{E_j}|f'|_k^2\,dS\\
 &\leq C_p\,2^{-j(4-p)/2}.
 \end{split}
\]
This is summable in $j$. On the remaining compact interior disc the
derivative is bounded, so $|f'|_k\in L^p(\mathbb D)$.

For completeness, the asserted Sobolev regularity is understood in
local target coordinates. Continuity on $\overline\mathbb D$ allows a finite
cover of the closed source disc by small neighborhoods whose images
lie in relatively compact target charts. In each such chart, the
coordinate functions are bounded, are smooth in the source interior,
and have first derivatives in $L^p$ by the estimate just proved and
metric comparison. These classical derivatives are their weak
derivatives, as is seen by testing against compactly supported smooth
functions in the source interior. Hence the coordinate functions lie
in $W^{1,p}$ up to the boundary, with the continuous boundary values
already constructed. This proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The constants in Proposition~\ref{amp:app:ex:regularity} need not be uniform
in $k$, $q$, or $\delta$. What will be used is the regularity of each
individual maximizing disc, to construct variations with unrestricted
boundary values. The constant $D$ in Lemma~\ref{amp:app:ex:brody}, in contrast,
depends only on the fixed metric $k$ and the compact manifold $X$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:var:initial-frame}
The bundle $f^*T^{1,0}X$ admits a holomorphic frame $e$ on $\mathbb D$ which
extends to a continuous, nonsingular $W^{1,p}$ frame on $\overline\mathbb D$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
In a nonsingular $W^{1,p}$ frame the pulled-back Dolbeault operator
is $\bar\partial+a$, with $a\in L^p$. The local Cauchy-transform
gauges and holomorphic gluing in Appendix~\ref{amp:calc:initial-frame}
produce an invertible $W^{1,p}$ solution of $\bar\partial U=-aU$
on the closed disc. Multiplying the initial frame by $U$ proves the
claim without extending $f$ across the boundary.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:var:frame}
Let $k$ be a smooth Hermitian metric on $X$.  There exist a number
$p_0$ with $2<p_0\le p$ and a holomorphic frame
$B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ of $f^*T^{1,0}X$ which is continuous,
nonsingular, and $W^{1,p_0}$ on $\overline\mathbb D$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{amp:app:var:boundary-unitary}
 B(z)^*k(f(z))B(z)=I,
 \qquad z\in\partial\mathbb D.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
In the boundary-regular frame $e$, the positive matrix $M=e^*k(f)e$
belongs to $W^{1,p}$. The weighted Hardy construction in
Appendix~\ref{amp:calc:boundary-frame} gives a bounded holomorphic
factor $S$, nonsingular in the interior, with $S^*MS=I$ almost
everywhere on the boundary. The rotation estimate there gives
$S\in H^s(S^1)$ for $1/2<s<1-1/p$, and its Fourier estimates give
$S\in W^{1,p_0}$ for $2<p_0<2/(3/2-s)$, $p_0\le p$.
Thus $S$ is continuous on the closed disc; the boundary identity
then holds everywhere and implies boundary nonsingularity.
The frame $B=eS$ has the stated properties. Boundary
nonsingularity is obtained after, not assumed before, this regularity.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:var:spray}
Let $B$ and $p_0>2$ be as in Proposition~\ref{amp:app:var:frame}, and set
$x=f(0)$.  For some $\eta>0$, there is a map
\[
 F\colon\{t\in\mathbb C^n:|t|<\eta\}\times\overline\mathbb D\longrightarrow X
\]
which is continuous on its domain and jointly holomorphic on
$\{|t|<\eta\}\times\mathbb D$, and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{amp:app:var:spray-identities}
 F(0,z)=f(z),\qquad F(t,0)=x,\qquad
 \frac{\partial F}{\partial t_j}(0,z)=z b_j(z).
\end{equation}
In fixed local target coordinates covering the graph of $f$, the
maps $t\mapsto F(t,\cdot)$ are holomorphic with values in
$W^{1,p_0}$ on the corresponding source patches.  In particular
every $F(t,\cdot)$ is a finite-area holomorphic disc centered at $x$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The construction in Appendix~\ref{amp:calc:centered-variations}
provides fiberwise holomorphic coordinates with inverse $E(z,\xi)$
near the graph, normalized by $E(z,0)=f(z)$ and $E_\xi(z,0)=e(z)$.
Its Sobolev substitution estimates make the holomorphic-map equation
$\bar\partial u+Q(z,u)=0$ a holomorphic Banach-space equation,
with $Q(z,0)=Q_\xi(z,0)=0$. For $B=eS$, the centered Cauchy right
inverse $Hg=Tg-(Tg)(0)$ solves
\[
 u=zS(z)t-HQ(\cdot,u)
\]
by contraction, holomorphically in $t$. Thus $F(t,z)=E(z,u(t,z))$
has the prescribed center and derivatives. The same estimates give
continuity on the closed product and holomorphic $W^{1,p_0}$
parameter dependence; separate holomorphy yields joint holomorphy
in the interior. Since $p_0>2$, the discs have finite area.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:var:center-derivative}
Although derivative evaluation at a point is not bounded on the full
space $W^{1,p_0}$, it is bounded on its holomorphic subspace on each
smaller disc, by the Cauchy formula.  In particular
$t\mapsto \partial_zF(t,0)$ is holomorphic.  Hence the central
derivative functional can be differentiated along
Proposition~\ref{amp:app:var:spray} without additional boundary regularity.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:hes:determinant}
With these conventions,
\begin{equation}\label{amp:app:eq:determinant-identity}
 \log\det N(0)=P_{\mathsf r_k}(f).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
In a holomorphic target chart, the matrix of $B$ is holomorphic and
nonsingular. Thus
\[
 \partial_z\partial_{\bar z}\log\det N
 =\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}\log\det k(f(z))
 =-\mathsf r_k(f',f').
\]
The first equality follows because $\log|\det B|^2$ is harmonic; the
formula is independent of the target chart. The right-hand side lies
in $L^{p_0/2}$. Apply Lemma~\ref{amp:app:pre:green} and use
$\log\det N=0$ on the boundary.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:hes:trace}
For every smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $q$,
\begin{align}
 \mathscr L_{\!\mathrm{var}} d(f_t)&=\operatorname{tr}(B(0)^*k(x)B(0)),\label{amp:app:eq:hessian-central}\\
 \mathscr L_{\!\mathrm{var}} P_q(f_t)&=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
      (\operatorname{tr}_k q)(f(e^{i\theta}))\,\mathrm d\theta.\label{amp:app:eq:hessian-poisson}
\end{align}
Here $f_t(z)=F(t,z)$ denotes the disc; variation vectors are written
$\partial_{t_j}F(0,z)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
\textbf{The central term and differentiation under the integrals.}
Since $F(t,0)=x$, the vector $\partial_z F(t,0)$ is holomorphic in $t$
and lies in the fixed vector space $T_x^{1,0}X$. Its $t_j$ derivative
at zero is $b_j(0)$. Differentiating its squared $k(x)$ norm gives
Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:hessian-central}. The holomorphic dependence of this
central derivative also follows directly from Cauchy's formula on a
smaller source circle.

We next justify the variations under the area and Poisson integrals.
Choose finitely many fixed source patches and target charts containing
the image of $F$ for sufficiently small $t$. In each chart the map
$t\mapsto F(t,\cdot)$ is holomorphic into $W^{1,p_0}$. The smooth metric
coefficients and the product rule imply that
\[
 t\longmapsto q(F_z(t,\cdot),F_z(t,\cdot))
\]
is twice continuously differentiable into $L^{p_0/2}$; the same holds
with $k$. Indeed, each parameter derivative is a sum of products of two
first source derivatives in $L^{p_0}$, with uniformly bounded Sobolev
coefficient factors. A fixed partition of unity in the source gives the
global assertion. Since $p_0/2>1$, integration against $1$ or against
$\log(1/|z|)$ is a continuous functional on this space. Differentiation
under both integrals is therefore valid.

\paragraph{The local identity and its Poisson integral.}
Locally write $q=i\partial\bar\partial\phi$. Joint holomorphy of $F$ on the open product
of the parameter domain and the disc gives
\begin{align*}
 q(F_z,F_z)&=\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}(\phi\circ F),\\
 \mathscr L_{\!\mathrm{var}}(\phi\circ F)&=\sum_j q(\partial_{t_j}F,\partial_{t_j}F)\big|_{t=0}.
\end{align*}
Commuting these derivatives and using $\partial_{t_j}F(0,z)=zb_j(z)$ yields the
intrinsic identity
\begin{equation}\label{amp:app:eq:local-hessian}
 \mathscr L_{\!\mathrm{var}} q(F_z,F_z)
 =\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}
     \left(|z|^2\operatorname{tr}(B^*q(f)B)\right).
\end{equation}
In particular, the mixed source derivative on the right belongs to
$L^{p_0/2}$ by the preceding differentiability argument.

The scalar function in parentheses is continuous on $\overline\mathbb D$ and
vanishes at zero. Lemma~\ref{amp:app:pre:green} therefore computes its Poisson
integral from its boundary values. On the boundary, the columns of $B$
are a $k$-orthonormal basis, so
$\operatorname{tr}(B^*qB)=\operatorname{tr}_k q$. This proves
Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:hessian-poisson}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:hes:hermitian}
For any smooth Hermitian metric $k$ and the above variations, put
\[
 \mathcal B_k(f,B)=\frac1\pi\int_\mathbb D\sum_j
 \mathcal C(zb_j,f',\overline{zb_j},\overline{f'})\,\mathrm d S,
\]
where $\mathcal C$ is the tensor just defined. Then
\begin{equation}\label{amp:app:eq:hessian-area}
 \mathscr L_{\!\mathrm{var}} A_k(f_t)=n-A_{\mathsf r_k}(f)+A_\Lambda(f)+\mathcal B_k(f,B).
\end{equation}
If $i\partial\bar\partial k\le0$ weakly on decomposable complex bivectors, then
$\mathcal B_k\le0$ and hence
$\mathscr L_{\!\mathrm{var}} A_k\le n-A_{\mathsf r_k}+A_\Lambda$.
All boundary passages in this identity are valid for continuous
$W^{1,p_0}$ frames and discs with $p_0>2$; boundary derivative traces
are not assumed.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
For one variation write $w=f'$ and $V=\partial_tF(0,z)$, and put
$S=\langle T(V,w),V\rangle_k$.  Direct differentiation, without a local potential
for $k$, gives
\[
 \partial_t\partial_{\bar t}\langle F_z,F_z\rangle_k|_0
 -\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}\langle V,V\rangle_k
 =\mathcal C(V,w,\bar V,\bar w)
       +\partial_{\bar z}S+\partial_z\bar S.
\]
The tensor $\mathcal C$ is the Hermitian form of $i\partial\bar\partial\omega_k$ on
decomposable bivectors, so its bulk contribution is nonpositive under
plurinegativity.  Sum this identity over $V_j=zb_j$ and integrate.
The trace term yields $n-A_{\mathsf r_k}(f)$, and the torsion
divergence yields $A_\Lambda(f)$.

For these last passages one cannot assume boundary derivative traces.
Instead, $N=B^*k(f)B$ satisfies
$\|N(r,\cdot)-I\|_2=o(\sqrt{1-r})$.  Integrability of the radial
squared norms of $N_r$ and $w$ gives one sequence $r\uparrow1$ on
which both
$\|N-I\|_2\|N_r\|_2$ and $\|N-I\|_2\|w\|_2$ tend to zero.
It simultaneously replaces the radial trace derivative by that of
$\log\det N$ and the frame-weighted torsion trace by $\eta(w)$.
All interior terms are in $L^{p_0/2}$, so their full-disc integrals
have sequence-independent limits.  This proves the stated exact
identity and its upper bound.
The detailed calculation is given in Appendix~\ref{amp:calc:hermitian-area}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:hes:maximum}
For a maximizer of $d+P_q-\delta A_k$, with $q$ closed,
\begin{equation}\label{amp:app:eq:maximum-inequality}
 \operatorname{tr} N(0)+\langle(\operatorname{tr}_k q)\circ f\rangle_1
 \le\delta\bigl(n-A_{\mathsf r_k}(f)+A_\Lambda(f)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Also $\log\det N(0)=P_{\mathsf r_k}(f)$ and $A_q(f)\ge-d(f)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Every small complex parameter value is an admissible centered
finite-area disc. Thus $\mathscr L_{\!\mathrm{var}}(d+P_q-\delta A_k)(f_t)\le0$.
Use the two trace identities, the upper area-Hessian inequality,
the determinant identity and
Lemma~\ref{amp:app:ex:dilation}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:nef:disc-bound}
There is $C_*<\infty$ depending only on $(X,k)$ such that
$P_{\mathsf r_k}(g)\le C_*$ for every finite-area holomorphic disc $g$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Fix $0<\delta\le1$ and a center and let $f$ maximize
$J_\delta=d+P_{\mathsf r_k}-\delta A_k$. Put $P=P_{\mathsf r_k}(f)$,
$M=\sup_X|\operatorname{tr}_k\mathsf r_k|$, and $C\ge0$ with $|\Lambda|\le Ck$.
Comparison with the constant disc gives
\[
 \delta A_k(f)\le d(f)+P\le D+P,\qquad P\ge-D.
\]
Dilation gives $A_{\mathsf r_k}(f)\ge-D$. Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{tr} N(0)&\le\delta(n-A_{\mathsf r_k}+A_\Lambda)+M\\
 &\le n+D+M+C(D+P)=:C_0+CP.
\end{align*}
The determinant identity and the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality
imply
\[
 n e^{P/n}\le\operatorname{tr} N(0)\le C_0+CP.
\]
This is an exponential versus linear bound, even if $C$ is large.
If $P\le0$ no upper estimate is needed. If $P\ge0$, use
$e^{P/n}\ge P^2/(2n^2)$ to get
\[
 P\le B:=nC+\sqrt{n^2C^2+2nC_0}.
\]
Consequently $J_\delta(f)\le D+B$ independently of the center
and $\delta$. Given an arbitrary \emph{fixed} finite-area disc $g$,
maximize at its center and obtain
\[
 d(g)+P_{\mathsf r_k}(g)-\delta A_k(g)\le D+B.
\]
Let $\delta\downarrow0$ for that disc. Since $d(g)\ge0$,
$P_{\mathsf r_k}(g)\le D+B=:C_*$. No uniform area bound for the
maximizing discs as $\delta\to0$ is asserted or used.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{amp:app:nef:bounded-potentials}
There is a bounded real-valued function $u$ on $X$ such that
\[
 T=-\mathsf r_k+i\partial\bar\partial u\geq0
\]
is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current.  In every local holomorphic
frame $s_i$ of $\det T^{1,0}X$, put $a_i=\log|s_i|_k^2$.
Then $a_i+u$ is plurisubharmonic and locally bounded.  These are
local weights of a singular Hermitian metric with nonnegative
curvature on $K_X$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Write $L=\det T^{1,0}X$ and let $\pi:Y=L\setminus 0_X\to X$ be
the complement of its zero section.  Define
\[
 \ell(s)=\log|s|_k^2,\qquad s\in Y.
\]
This is a smooth finite-valued function on the connected complex
manifold $Y$.  In a local trivialization $s=\lambda s_i(x)$ it has
the expression
\[
 \ell(s)=\log|\lambda|^2+a_i(x),\qquad
 i\partial\bar\partial a_i=-\mathsf r_k.
\]
Since $\lambda\ne0$, the first summand is pluriharmonic.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 i\partial\bar\partial\ell=-\pi^*\mathsf r_k.
 \label{amp:app:eq:nef-total-space-curvature}
\end{equation}

Let $v=\mathcal P\ell$, using test discs holomorphic past the closed
unit disc.  For such a disc $G$ with $G(0)=s$, its projection
$f=\pi\circ G$ has finite area.  Green's formula and
Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:nef-total-space-curvature} give
\[
 \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\ell(G(e^{i\theta}))\,\mathrm d\theta
 =\ell(s)-P_{\mathsf r_k}(f).
\]
Put $C=C_*$. Proposition~\ref{amp:app:nef:disc-bound} bounds every such mean below by
$\ell(s)-C$, while the constant disc has mean $\ell(s)$.  Thus
\begin{equation}
 \ell-C\leq v\leq\ell.
 \label{amp:app:eq:nef-envelope-bounds}
\end{equation}
The Poletsky--Rosay Theorem applies even though $\ell$ is globally
unbounded, and Equation~\eqref{amp:app:eq:nef-envelope-bounds} excludes its
identically $-\infty$ alternative.  Hence $v$ is plurisubharmonic.

For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C^*$, multiplication by $\lambda$ is a
biholomorphism of $Y$ and gives a bijection between the test discs
centered at $s$ and at $\lambda s$.  Since
$\ell(\lambda s)=\ell(s)+\log|\lambda|^2$, it follows that
\[
 v(\lambda s)=v(s)+\log|\lambda|^2.
\]
Thus $v-\ell$ is constant on every fiber.  It has the form
$u\circ\pi$, where $-C\leq u\leq0$.  Pulling back $v$ by the local
holomorphic map $s_i$ proves that $a_i+u$ is plurisubharmonic.
It is locally bounded because $a_i$ is smooth and $u$ is bounded.
The local currents $i\partial\bar\partial(a_i+u)$ agree and equal $-\mathsf r_k+i\partial\bar\partial u$.

To check the line-bundle sign explicitly, if $s_i=g_{ij}s_j$ then
\[
 a_i-a_j=\log|g_{ij}|^2.
\]
Let $s_i^*$ be the dual frame of $K_X=L^*$.  The prescription
\[
 |s_i^*|^2=\exp\bigl(-(a_i+u)\bigr)
\]
is compatible with $s_i^*=g_{ij}^{-1}s_j^*$.  Its curvature is
$i\partial\bar\partial(a_i+u)=T\geq0$.  In particular $T$ represents
$2\pi c_1(K_X)$, rather than $2\pi c_1(L)$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{amp:lem:zero-lelong-nef}
Let $M$ be compact complex, let $\omega$ be a smooth Hermitian form,
and let $\alpha$ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form. If
$T=\alpha+i\partial\bar\partial u\ge0$ has bounded potential $u$, then, for each
$\varepsilon>0$, there is $v_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ such that
$\alpha+i\partial\bar\partial v_\varepsilon\ge-\varepsilon\omega$. Thus $[\alpha]$ is analytically nef.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Locally, $T$ has bounded plurisubharmonic potentials, so
$\nu(T,x)=0$ at every point. Choose $A\ge0$ sufficiently large that
the Chern curvature of $(T^{1,0}M,\omega)$ is bounded below by
$-A\omega\otimes\operatorname{Id}$. Demailly's regularization theorem
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{amp:new:Demailly1994}, with its curvature-bound
form equal to $A\omega$, supplies smooth representatives
\[
 T_j=\alpha+i\partial\bar\partial v_j\ge-(A\lambda_j+\delta_j)\omega,
\]
where $\delta_j\to0$ and the continuous functions $\lambda_j$ decrease
pointwise to $\nu(T,\cdot)=0$. Dini's theorem gives
$\|\lambda_j\|_\infty\to0$. Choosing $j$ sufficiently large proves
the assertion. Neither $d\omega=0$ nor continuity of $u$ is needed.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{amp:prop:entrance}\label{amp:app:cor:bounded-canonical}
There is a finite $G$ with $P_{\operatorname{Ric}_k^{(1)}}(f)\le G$ for all
finite-area holomorphic discs. Moreover, for
$\alpha_k=-\operatorname{Ric}_k^{(1)}$ there is a bounded real potential $u$ with
$\alpha_k+i\partial\bar\partial u\ge0$, and $K_X$ is nef.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{amp:app:nef:disc-bound} supplies $G$.
Proposition~\ref{amp:app:nef:bounded-potentials} constructs the bounded
positive canonical potential. Lemma~\ref{amp:lem:zero-lelong-nef}
then proves nefness. The bounded potential comes from the envelope
construction; the later argument needs only nefness to choose
smooth almost-positive representatives.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{amp:lem:penalty}
Let $F$ be a real function on a set $S$ with finite supremum $M_0$,
and let $A:S\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. Suppose
$M_\delta=\sup_S(F-\delta A)$ is attained at $s_\delta$ for each
$\delta>0$. Then
\[
 M_\delta\uparrow M_0,\qquad
 0\le\delta A(s_\delta)\le M_0-M_\delta\longrightarrow0
 \quad(\delta\downarrow0).
\]
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The upper bound $M_\delta\le M_0$ is immediate. Each fixed $s\in S$
gives $M_\delta\ge F(s)-\delta A(s)$, so the lower limit is at least
$\sup_S F=M_0$. At a maximizer,
$\delta A(s_\delta)=F(s_\delta)-M_\delta\le M_0-M_\delta$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{amp:prop:uniform-volume}
Every smooth plurinegative Hermitian metric $\beta$ on $X$ satisfying
$\operatorname{Ric}_\beta^{(1)}\ge-\beta$ obeys
\begin{equation}\label{amp:eq:uniform-volume}
 \beta^n\ge e^{-D}k^n.
\end{equation}
The constant does not depend on any derivative or torsion bound for $\beta$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Fix $\beta$ and $x\in X$. Maximize, on finite-area discs with center $x$,
\[
 J_\delta(f)=d_k(f)+P_{\operatorname{Ric}_\beta^{(1)}}(f)-\delta A_\beta(f).
\]
The proof in Section~\ref{amp:app:sec:extremal-discs} applies with reward measured by $k$ and area
measured by $\beta$: compactness compares fixed metrics; the interior
normal-family estimates and the domination of the logarithmic term
by the area penalty on a boundary collar are unchanged. It supplies
an actual maximizer $f_\delta$, continuous on the closed disc and
$W^{1,p}$ for $p>2$. All intermediate constants may depend on the
fixed $\beta$, $\delta$, and $x$.

By \eqref{amp:eq:ricci-transfer}, the unpenalized supremum is finite. Lemma~\ref{amp:lem:penalty}
therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{amp:eq:penalty-limit}
 \delta A_\beta(f_\delta)\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Choose the boundary-$\beta$-unitary holomorphic frame $B_\delta$
and the centered variations of Section~\ref{amp:app:var:section}. Put
\[
 \tau_\delta=\operatorname{tr}(B_\delta(0)^*k(x)B_\delta(0)),\qquad
 N_\delta=B_\delta^*\beta(f_\delta)B_\delta.
\]
The central Hessian uses $k(x)$ because the center is fixed; the
Poisson term uses the boundary $\beta$-orthonormality. Section~\ref{amp:app:sec:hessian},
with its favorable plurinegative bulk, gives
\begin{equation}\label{amp:eq:volume-trace}
 \tau_\delta+\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
  (\operatorname{tr}_\beta\operatorname{Ric}_\beta^{(1)})(f_\delta(e^{i\theta}))\,\mathrm d\theta
 \le\delta\bigl(n-A_{\operatorname{Ric}_\beta^{(1)}}(f_\delta)
                         +A_{\Lambda_\beta}(f_\delta)\bigr).
\end{equation}
This is a two-metric use of the same proved variation identities, not
a replacement of the frame metric inside the area Hessian.

For this fixed smooth $\beta$, compactness gives
$|\Lambda_\beta|\le C_\beta\beta$. Also
$\operatorname{tr}_\beta\operatorname{Ric}_\beta^{(1)}\ge-n$ and $-A_{\operatorname{Ric}_\beta^{(1)}}\le A_\beta$.
Consequently
\[
 \tau_\delta\le n+\delta n+(1+C_\beta)\delta A_\beta(f_\delta),
 \qquad\limsup_{\delta\downarrow0}\tau_\delta\le n.
\]
The constant disc has value zero, so
\[
 P_{\operatorname{Ric}_\beta^{(1)}}(f_\delta)
 \ge\delta A_\beta(f_\delta)-d_k(f_\delta)\ge-D.
\]
The determinant identity and arithmetic--geometric mean now imply
\[
 \frac{\beta^n}{k^n}(x)
 =\frac{\det(B_\delta(0)^*\beta(x)B_\delta(0))}
        {\det(B_\delta(0)^*k(x)B_\delta(0))}
 \ge e^{-D}\left(\frac n{\tau_\delta}\right)^n.
\]
The ratio on the left is independent of $\delta$. Letting $\delta$
decrease to zero proves the assertion at $x$. No limiting disc,
uniform boundary derivative estimate, or uniform control of
$C_\beta$ is needed. This limit is taken separately for each fixed
metric and each point.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{amp:thm:hermitian-cma}
For any compact Hermitian manifold $(X,\omega)$, any smooth real $F$
and any $\lambda>0$, there is a unique smooth real $\phi$ satisfying
\[
 \omega+i\partial\bar\partial\phi>0,\qquad
 \log\frac{(\omega+i\partial\bar\partial\phi)^n}{\omega^n}=\lambda\phi+F.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{amp:lem:bounded-cma-morse}
Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on a compact complex manifold,
let $\alpha$ be the smooth real curvature of a metric on $L$, and let
$k,h$ be smooth Hermitian forms. Suppose smooth real $u_\varepsilon$ satisfy
\[
 \beta_\varepsilon=\alpha+\varepsilon k+i\partial\bar\partial u_\varepsilon>0,\quad
 \beta_\varepsilon^n=e^{u_\varepsilon}h^n,\quad
 \beta_\varepsilon^n\ge b k^n
\]
for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ and a fixed $b>0$.
Then $\int_X\alpha^n\ge b\int_Xk^n>0$ and $L$ is big.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The determinant equation gives
$u_\varepsilon\ge\log b+\log(k^n/h^n)$. At its maximum,
$0<\beta_\varepsilon\le\alpha+\varepsilon k\le C h$ for one fixed $C\ge1$
and $0<\varepsilon\le1$, so $u_\varepsilon\le n\log C$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{amp:eq:cma-bounded}
 \|u_\varepsilon\|_\infty\le C_1.
\end{equation}

Choose finitely many coordinate balls $V_j\Subset U_j$ covering $X$.
On each $U_j$, choose a fixed quadratic function $\rho_j$ with
$i\partial\bar\partial\rho_j\ge\alpha+k$, and write $\omega_{0,j}=i\partial\bar\partial|z|^2$.
Then the uniformly bounded functions $p_{j,\varepsilon}=u_\varepsilon+\rho_j$ are
plurisubharmonic and
\[
 0<\beta_\varepsilon\le Q_{j,\varepsilon}:=i\partial\bar\partial p_{j,\varepsilon},\qquad
 k\le C_j\omega_{0,j}.
\]
Here the comparison is local; $\beta_\varepsilon$ need not be closed.

For clarity, the local Chern--Levine--Nirenberg estimate needed here
has a short proof. Add a constant to a bounded smooth psh function
$p$ so that $0\le p\le M$. Choose nested cutoffs $\chi$, with
$\chi=1$ on successive smaller sets and support on the next larger
set. Since $i\partial\bar\partial p$ and the Euclidean $\omega_0$ are closed,
\[
 \int\chi(i\partial\bar\partial p)^r\wedge\omega_0^{n-r}
 =\int p\,i\partial\bar\partial\chi\wedge(i\partial\bar\partial p)^{r-1}\wedge\omega_0^{n-r}
 \le C M\int_{\operatorname{supp}\chi}
              (i\partial\bar\partial p)^{r-1}\wedge\omega_0^{n-r+1}.
\]
The last inequality uses $i\partial\bar\partial\chi\le C\omega_0$ and positivity.
Iterating to $r=0$ proves a bound depending only on the fixed domains
and $M$. The uniform bounds in \eqref{amp:eq:cma-bounded}, positivity,
and the finite cover therefore give, for every $0\le r\le n$,
\begin{equation}\label{amp:eq:cma-mixed}
 \int_X\beta_\varepsilon^r\wedge k^{n-r}\le C_r.
\end{equation}

Set $\theta_\varepsilon=\alpha+i\partial\bar\partial u_\varepsilon=\beta_\varepsilon-\varepsilon k$.
This is a closed curvature form on $L$. Expansion and
\eqref{amp:eq:cma-mixed} give
\[
 \left|\int_X\beta_\varepsilon^n-\int_X\theta_\varepsilon^n\right|\le C\varepsilon.
\]
Stokes gives $\int_X\theta_\varepsilon^n=\int_X\alpha^n$, hence the stated
positive lower bound follows by sending $\varepsilon$ to zero.

To verify bigness on the still possibly non-K\"ahler manifold, set
$P_\varepsilon=\theta_\varepsilon+2\varepsilon k=\beta_\varepsilon+\varepsilon k>0$.
If $\lambda_i$ are the $k$-eigenvalues of $\theta_\varepsilon$, then
$\lambda_i\ge-\varepsilon$. On the locus with a negative eigenvalue,
\[
 \left|\prod_i\lambda_i\right|
 \le\varepsilon\sum_j\prod_{i\ne j}(\lambda_i+2\varepsilon),\qquad
 |\theta_\varepsilon^n|\le n\varepsilon P_\varepsilon^{n-1}\wedge k.
\]
Its total absolute mass is $O(\varepsilon)$ by \eqref{amp:eq:cma-mixed}.
For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta$, let $X(\theta,\le1)$
denote the nondegenerate locus where $\theta$ has at most one
negative eigenvalue, counted with respect to any Hermitian metric.
This is the Morse signature locus. On the degenerate locus
$\theta^n=0$, so that locus contributes no top-degree mass. Thus
\[
 \int_{X(\theta_\varepsilon,\le1)}\theta_\varepsilon^n
 \ge\int_X\alpha^n-C\varepsilon>0
\]
for a sufficiently small fixed $\varepsilon$. The smooth metric on $L$
obtained by multiplying the original one by $e^{-u_\varepsilon}$ has exactly
curvature $\theta_\varepsilon$. The strong holomorphic Morse inequality
\cite[Theorem 0.1 and equation (0.7)]{amp:old:Demailly1985} yields
\[
 h^0(X,L^m)-h^1(X,L^m)
 \ge\frac{m^n}{n!(2\pi)^n}
       \int_{X(\theta_\varepsilon,\le1)}\theta_\varepsilon^n+o(m^n).
\]
Consequently $h^0(X,L^m)\ge c m^n$ for large $m$, proving bigness.
The parameter $\varepsilon$ was fixed before $m\to\infty$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Hyperbolicity excludes rational curves: a nonconstant map
$\mathbb P^1\to X$ would remain nonconstant on $\mathbb C$.
The big canonical bundle makes $X$ Moishezon, hence in class
$\mathcal C$. Lemma~\ref{n:lem:no-rational-kahler} makes $X$
K\"ahler, and a K\"ahler Moishezon manifold is projective
\cite{amp:old:Moishezon1967}; see also \cite[Theorem~6]{amp:new:Namikawa}.

For completeness, the projective implication ``big canonical bundle
and no rational curves imply ample'' can be proved directly
\cite[Lemma 2.1]{amp:new:DT}. Kodaira's lemma supplies an integer $m>0$,
an ample divisor $H$ and an effective divisor $E$ with
$mK_X\sim H+E$. For sufficiently small positive rational $t$, the
pair $(X,tE)$ is klt. If $K_X+tE$ were not nef, the log cone theorem
would produce a rational curve, a contradiction. Put $N=K_X+tE$;
then
\[
 (1+tm)K_X\sim_{\mathbb Q}N+tH
\]
is ample, since a nef plus an ample rational divisor is ample.
Clearing denominators proves that $K_X$ is ample. No abundance
conjecture or dimension restriction is used.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The strict negative bound is uniform by compactness. The Hermitian
Ahlfors--Schwarz argument in Lemma~\ref{amp:app:pre:hyperbolic}
excludes nonconstant entire curves, so Theorem~\ref{amp:main} applies.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{n:lem:fujiki-kahler}
Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, and let
$h$ be a Hermitian metric satisfying $H_h\le0$.
Then $X$ contains no rational curve.  Consequently $X$ is K\"ahler.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Suppose that $\varphi:\mathbb P^1\to X$ is a nonconstant holomorphic map. Choose a
Fubini--Study metric $\gamma$ on $\mathbb P^1$ and set
\[
 \operatorname{Ric}_\gamma=\rho\,\omega_\gamma,\qquad \rho>0,
 \qquad w=|\partial \varphi|^2_{\gamma,h}.
\]
At every point where $d\varphi\ne0$, the rank-one Chern--Lu formula for a
holomorphic map from a K\"ahler curve to a Hermitian target gives
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:rank-one-cl-fujiki}
\Delta_\gamma w
\ge \rho w-H_h(d\varphi)w^2.
\end{equation}
Since the source has complex dimension one, the target curvature term is
the Chern holomorphic sectional curvature of the line spanned by $d\varphi$.
At a positive maximum of $w$, the assumption $H_h\le0$ gives
$\Delta_\gamma w\ge\rho w>0$, a contradiction. Thus $w\equiv0$,
and $X$ contains no rational curve.

Lemma~\ref{n:lem:no-rational-kahler} now implies that $X$ is K\"ahler.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{n:lem:ICL}
Let $X$ be compact of complex dimension $n\ge2$, let $g$ be K\"ahler, and let $h$ be Hermitian with $H_h\equiv c$. Suppose
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_g^{(1)}=a_0\,\omega_g,
\]
where $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Put
\[
 u=\operatorname{tr}_g h,\qquad q=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((g^{-1}h)^2\bigr).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:icl-pointwise}
\Delta_g u
=|\mathsf S|^2+a_0 u-\frac c2(u^2+q)+\frac14\mathcal D_g,
\end{equation}
where $\mathsf S$ is the symmetric part of $\nabla^h-\nabla^g$. Its norm uses
$g$ on the two covariant slots and $h$ on the output:
\[
 |\mathsf S|^2=g^{i\bar j}g^{k\bar\ell}h_{p\bar q}
 \mathsf S^p{}_{ik}\overline{\mathsf S^q{}_{j\ell}}.
\]
We set
\[
\mathcal D_g=g^{i\bar j}g^{k\bar\ell}
D_{i\bar j k\bar\ell}
\]
with $D$ normalized in holomorphic coordinates by
\begin{equation}
D_{i\bar j k\bar\ell}
=\partial_i\partial_{\bar j}h_{k\bar\ell}
+\partial_k\partial_{\bar\ell}h_{i\bar j}
-\partial_i\partial_{\bar\ell}h_{k\bar j}
-\partial_k\partial_{\bar j}h_{i\bar\ell}.
\label{n:eq:D-coordinate}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the ordered exterior-form convention is
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:D-ordered-form}
i\partial\bar\partial\omega_h
=\sum_{\substack{i<k\\j<\ell}}
D_{i\bar j k\bar\ell}\,
dz^i\wedge dz^k\wedge d\bar z^j\wedge d\bar z^\ell.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:D-wedge}
\mathcal D_g\,dV_g
=2\,i\partial\bar\partial\omega_h
\wedge\frac{\omega_g^{n-2}}{(n-2)!},
\end{equation}
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:D-integral-zero}
\int_X\mathcal D_g\,dV_g=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Put
\[
 \mathfrak s_g=g^{i\bar j}g^{k\bar\ell}R^h_{i\bar j k\bar\ell},\qquad
 \mathcal T=g^{i\bar j}g^{k\bar\ell}h_{p\bar q}
 T^p_{ik}\overline{T^q_{j\ell}}.
\]
The curvature expansion in Appendix~\ref{app:icl-calculations}
retains the full $i\partial\bar\partial\omega_h$ term.
Contracting \eqref{n:eq:general-tang} gives
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:Q-contraction}
\mathfrak s_g=\frac c2(u^2+q)+\frac14\mathcal T-\frac14\mathcal D_g.
\end{equation}

For the holomorphic identity map $\operatorname{Id}:(X,g)\to(X,h)$, equip its
differential with the connection induced by $g$ on the source and $h$ on
the target. The Chern--Lu formula, with $g$ K\"ahler, reads
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:chern-lu-before-cancel}
\Delta_g u
=|\nabla\partial\operatorname{Id}|^2
+\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(g^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g^{(1)}g^{-1}h\bigr)-\mathfrak s_g.
\end{equation}
Since the source metric $g$ is
K\"ahler, its Chern torsion vanishes.  The skew part in the two holomorphic
indices of $\nabla\partial\operatorname{Id}$ is therefore $T/2$.  If $\mathsf S$ denotes its
symmetric part, then the symmetric and skew parts are orthogonal, with the stated tensor norm
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:S-T-splitting}
|\nabla\partial\operatorname{Id}|^2=|\mathsf S|^2+\frac14\mathcal T.
\end{equation}
Substituting \eqref{n:eq:Q-contraction} and \eqref{n:eq:S-T-splitting} into
\eqref{n:eq:chern-lu-before-cancel} cancels the torsion contraction and gives
\eqref{n:eq:icl-pointwise}.

The exterior coefficient calculation in
Appendix~\ref{app:icl-calculations} proves \eqref{n:eq:D-wedge}.
Its factor $2$ occurs because the tensor contraction counts each
matching unordered index pair twice, whereas the ordered exterior
expression counts it once. Since $g$ is K\"ahler,
$\partial\omega_g=\bar\partial\omega_g=0$, and hence Stokes' theorem gives
\[
\int_X\mathcal D_g\,dV_g
=2\int_Xi\partial\bar\partial\omega_h
\wedge\frac{\omega_g^{n-2}}{(n-2)!}=0.
\]
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{n:lem:ample}
Let $X^n$ be compact K\"ahler, $n\ge2$, and let $h$ be a Hermitian
metric with $H_h\equiv c<0$. Then $K_X$ is ample.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The underlying manifold is K\"ahler, and the strictly negative
constant HSC of $h$ is quasi-negative. Apply
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{WanQuasiNegative2026}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{n:lem:comparison}
Let $X^n$ be compact, $n\ge2$, let $H_h\equiv c<0$, and let $g$ be a
K\"ahler metric with $\operatorname{Ric}_g^{(1)}=-\kappa\omega_g$, where
$b=-c/2>0$ and $\kappa=(n+1)b$. Then $h=g$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Put $M=g^{-1}h$, and let $\lambda_i>0$ be its eigenvalues. Write
\[
 u=\operatorname{tr} M,\quad v=\operatorname{tr} M^{-1},\quad q=\operatorname{tr} M^2,
 \qquad F=\log(dV_g/dV_h)=-\log\det M.
\]
The positive matrix function
\[
 \Phi(M)=\operatorname{tr} M-\log\det M-n
          =\sum_i(\lambda_i-1-\log\lambda_i)
\]
is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at $M=I$, by $\log x\le x-1$.
Thus $\Phi$ measures the failure of the two metrics to agree, including
changes of scale. Neither $u-n$ nor $v-n$ has a fixed sign separately;
the volume weights combine them into this matrix defect and its inverse.
The comparison expression therefore has the pointwise decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:metric-gap-decomposition}
 \mathscr G:=e^F(u-n)+e^{2F}(v-n)
 =e^F\Phi(M)+e^{2F}\Phi(M^{-1})+F(e^{2F}-e^F)\ge0.
\end{equation}
Its last term is nonnegative by monotonicity of the exponential.

We derive the weighted identity, including the choice of exponent.
For $\Theta_h=\omega_h^{n-1}/(n-1)!$, the torsion-trace identity gives
$\partial\Theta_h=-\eta\wedge\Theta_h$ and
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:ddbar-omega-nminus1}
 i\partial\bar\partial\Theta_h=(|\eta|_h^2-\chi)dV_h.
\end{equation}
Integration by parts, once and twice respectively, gives for real $\phi$
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:stokes-second}\label{n:eq:stokes-first}
 \int_X\Delta_h\phi\,dV_h
 =\operatorname{Re}\int_X\langle\partial\phi,\eta\rangle_h\,dV_h,\qquad \int_X\Delta_h\phi\,dV_h
 =\int_X\phi(|\eta|_h^2-\chi)dV_h.
\end{equation}
Here the first sign follows from
$i\bar\partial\phi\wedge\partial\Theta_h
=i\eta\wedge\bar\partial\phi\wedge\Theta_h$.
Taking the $h$-trace of
$i\partial\bar\partial F=\operatorname{Ric}_h^{(1)}-\operatorname{Ric}_g^{(1)}$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:lap-F-general}
 \Delta_hF=\kappa(v-n)+\chi/2.
\end{equation}
Apply both Stokes formulas to $e^{tF}$, $t>0$. With $x=\partial F$,
they imply
\begin{align}
 \int_Xe^{tF}(\Delta_hF+t|x|^2)dV_h
 &=\int_Xe^{tF}\operatorname{Re}\langle x,\eta\rangle_h dV_h,
       \label{n:eq:weighted-stokes-A}\\
 \int_Xe^{tF}\chi\,dV_h
 &=\int_Xe^{tF}(|\eta|^2-t\operatorname{Re}\langle x,\eta\rangle_h)dV_h.
       \label{n:eq:weighted-chi}
\end{align}
Substituting into \eqref{n:eq:lap-F-general} gives
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:weighted-master}
 \kappa\int_X e^{tF}(v-n)dV_h
 =\int_X e^{tF}\left[-t\left|x-\frac{t+2}{4t}\eta\right|^2
             +\frac{(t-2)^2}{16t}|\eta|^2\right]dV_h.
\end{equation}
The remainder vanishes precisely when $t=2$, so
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:t2-square}
 \kappa\int_X e^{2F}(v-n)dV_h
       =-2\int_Xe^{2F}|\partial F-\eta/2|^2dV_h.
\end{equation}

Lemma~\ref{n:lem:ICL} gives the second exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:comparison-icl}
 0=\int_X\left[|\mathsf S|^2+b\{u^2+q-(n+1)u\}\right]dV_g.
\end{equation}
The algebraic decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:trace-shift-squares}
 u^2+q-(n+1)u=(n+1)(u-n)+(u-n)^2+\sum_i(\lambda_i-1)^2
\end{equation}
and $dV_g=e^FdV_h$ now turn the sum of
\eqref{n:eq:t2-square} and \eqref{n:eq:comparison-icl} into
\begin{equation}\label{n:eq:combined-comparison}
\begin{aligned}
0={}&\kappa\int_X\mathscr G\,dV_h\\
 &+\int_X\left[|\mathsf S|^2+
 b\left((u-n)^2+\sum_i(\lambda_i-1)^2\right)\right]dV_g\\
 &+2\int_Xe^{2F}|\partial F-\eta/2|^2dV_h.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Each line is nonnegative and must vanish. The first gives
$\Phi(M)=0$, hence $h=g$, by \eqref{n:eq:metric-gap-decomposition}.
The second gives $\mathsf S=0$ and $\lambda_i=1$ for every $i$.
The third gives $\partial F=\eta/2$; since $h=g$ makes $F=0$,
it also gives $\eta=0$.
All expressions are invariant functions of $M$; no eigenframe is
differentiated in this argument.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{n:lem:fujiki-kahler}, the Fujiki-class manifold $X$ is K\"ahler.  We
may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{n:lem:ample}, which gives that $K_X$ is ample.  In
particular $X$ is projective by the Kodaira embedding theorem.  The
Aubin--Yau theorem \cite[Theorem~5, p.~385]{Yau} supplies the unique K\"ahler--Einstein
metric $g$ in the class
\[
[\omega_g]=\frac{2\pi}{-\lambda_c}c_1(K_X)
\]
with $\operatorname{Ric}_g^{(1)}=\lambda_c\omega_g$.  Then
Lemma~\ref{n:lem:comparison} gives $h=g$.  In particular $h$ is K\"ahler,
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_h^{(1)}=\lambda_c\omega_h,
\qquad
[\omega_h]=\frac{2\pi}{-\lambda_c}c_1(K_X).
\]
For a K\"ahler metric, constant holomorphic sectional curvature $c$
determines the full curvature tensor:
\[
R^h_{i\bar j k\bar\ell}
=\frac c2\bigl(h_{i\bar j}h_{k\bar\ell}+h_{i\bar\ell}h_{k\bar j}\bigr).
\]
Because $X$ is compact, $h$ is complete.  The complete simply connected
K\"ahler space-form classification
\cite[Chapter~IX, \S7, Theorem~7.9, pp.~170--171]{KN69}
therefore identifies the universal cover
with complex hyperbolic space of holomorphic sectional curvature $c$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{z:lem:parallel-endomorphism}
Let $(X,g)$ be a compact Ricci-flat K\"ahler manifold, and let
$D=\nabla^g$ denote its Chern connection and all induced tensor connections.
Suppose that $L$ is a smooth $g$-self-adjoint endomorphism of $T^{1,0}X$
satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{z:eq:symmetric-derivative-zero}
 D_iL^k{}_j+D_jL^k{}_i=0.
\end{equation}
Then $D L=0$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
We first show that the pure holomorphic Hessian vanishes, then use
Ricci-flatness and integration by parts to eliminate the first derivative.
Put
\[
 U_{rij}{}^k=D_rD_iL^k{}_j,
\]
where the second covariant derivative includes the connection on the
derivative index $i$. Since $g$ is K\"ahler, $D$ is torsion-free and
has no $(2,0)$-curvature. Hence $U$ is symmetric in $r,i$.
Differentiating \eqref{z:eq:symmetric-derivative-zero} shows that it is
skew-symmetric in $i,j$. These two symmetries give
\[
 U_{rij}{}^k=U_{irj}{}^k=-U_{ijr}{}^k
 =-U_{jir}{}^k=U_{jri}{}^k=U_{rji}{}^k=-U_{rij}{}^k.
\]
Thus $U=0$.

Regard $\mathsf J=D^{1,0}L$ as a section of the holomorphic Hermitian bundle
\[
 E=(T^{1,0}X)^*\otimes\operatorname{End}(T^{1,0}X),
\]
with all metrics, norms, and connections induced by $g$. The preceding calculation
is precisely $D^{1,0}\mathsf J=0$. The contracted curvature of $T^{1,0}X$
is the Ricci endomorphism of $g$. On $E$, curvature acts on the output
slot and with the opposite sign on each covariant slot. Contracting each
of these actions therefore gives zero, so
\[
 g^{a\bar b}R^E_{a\bar b}=0.
\]
For every smooth section $V$ of $E$, integration by parts and commutation
of the two covariant derivatives give
\[
 \|D^{1,0}V\|_{L^2(g)}^2
 -\|D^{0,1}V\|_{L^2(g)}^2
 =\operatorname{Re}\int_X
 \left\langle g^{a\bar b}R^E_{a\bar b}V,V\right\rangle_g\,dV_g
 =0.
\]
Here $R^E_{a\bar b}=[D_a,D_{\bar b}]$, in accordance with
the Chern curvature convention. Applying this identity to $V=\mathsf J$ gives
$D^{0,1}\mathsf J=0$, hence $D \mathsf J=0$.
In particular, $(D^{1,0})^*\mathsf J=0$. A final integration by parts yields
\[
 \|\mathsf J\|_{L^2(g)}^2
 =\operatorname{Re}\int_X\langle D^{1,0}L,\mathsf J\rangle_g\,dV_g
 =\operatorname{Re}\int_X
 \langle L,(D^{1,0})^*\mathsf J\rangle_g\,dV_g=0.
\]
Therefore $D^{1,0}L=0$. Since $D$ preserves $g$ and $L$ is
self-adjoint, taking adjoints also gives $D^{0,1}L=0$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{n:lem:fujiki-kahler}, the underlying manifold $X$ is
K\"ahler. Tang's theorem \cite[Theorem~1.1(2), p.~2]{TangNef}, applied to the
original Hermitian metric $h$, gives
$c_1(X)=0$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb R)$. Fix a K\"ahler form $\theta$ on the now K\"ahler manifold $X$.
The $\partial\bar\partial$ lemma gives a smooth real function $\zeta$ with
$\operatorname{Ric}(\theta)=i\partial\bar\partial \zeta$.
Choose its additive constant so that
\[
 \int_X e^\zeta\theta^n=\int_X\theta^n.
\]
Yau's theorem \cite[Theorem~1, p.~363; Theorem~2, p.~364]{Yau}
then solves
$(\theta+i\partial\bar\partial\varphi)^n=e^\zeta\theta^n$
with a positive K\"ahler form. Its Ricci form vanishes, so it defines
a Ricci-flat K\"ahler metric $g$ in the chosen class.
The Ricci form of $h$ is not used in this existence step.

Apply Lemma~\ref{n:lem:ICL} with $a_0=c=0$.
For $u=\operatorname{tr}_g h$ it gives
\begin{equation}\label{z:eq:icl-zero}
 \Delta_g u=|\mathsf S|^2+\frac14\mathcal D_g,
 \qquad
 \int_X\mathcal D_g\,dV_g=0.
\end{equation}
Integrating against $dV_g$ shows that $\mathsf S=0$ everywhere.
To express this as an equation for the metric, write $D=\nabla^g$ and
$K=\nabla^h-\nabla^g$. Since both Chern connections have the same
$(0,1)$ part, their holomorphic coefficients satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{z:eq:connection-difference}
 K^p{}_{ij}=h^{p\bar\ell}D_i h_{j\bar\ell},\qquad
 \mathsf S^p{}_{ij}
 =\frac12h^{p\bar\ell}
   \bigl(D_i h_{j\bar\ell}+D_j h_{i\bar\ell}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus $D_i h_{j\bar\ell}+D_j h_{i\bar\ell}=0$.
Define the positive $g$-self-adjoint endomorphism $L$ by
$\langle v,w\rangle_h=\langle Lv,w\rangle_g$. Since $Dg=0$, this last equation becomes
\[
 D_iL^k{}_j+D_jL^k{}_i=0.
\]
Lemma~\ref{z:lem:parallel-endomorphism} now gives $DL=0$, hence $Dh=0$.
The torsion-free connection $D$ preserves the complex structure and $h$;
therefore it preserves $\omega_h$, and alternating its covariant
derivative gives $d\omega_h=0$. The original metric $h$ is K\"ahler.
Only at this point may K\"ahler polarization be used: $H_h\equiv0$
then gives $R^h=0$.

Compactness makes $h$ complete, and
the lifted metric on the universal cover is complete as well.
The flat case of the complex space-form classification
\cite[Chapter~IX, \S7, Theorem~7.9 and p.~171]{KN69}
identifies that cover holomorphically and isometrically with $\mathbb C^n$.
Thus $X$ is $\mathbb C^n/\Gamma$, where
$\Gamma\subset U(n)\ltimes\mathbb C^n$ is a discrete, cocompact group
acting freely by deck transformations.
Bieberbach's translation theorem \cite{Bieberbach1911}, in the form
recalled in \cite[\S1, p.~401]{Bieberbach1912}, supplies $2n$ independent
translations: the underlying Euclidean action is discrete and cocompact.
Thus $\Lambda=\Gamma\cap\mathbb C^n$ is a normal full lattice.
The quotient $\Gamma/\Lambda$ embeds in its orthogonal automorphism
group, which is finite because the images of a lattice basis have
prescribed lengths and range over finite subsets of the lattice.
Consequently
$\mathbb C^n/\Lambda\to X$ is a finite \'etale cover by a complex torus,
and the lifted metric is translation invariant.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:decomp}
On a Hermitian threefold with $H_h\equiv c$, there are unique
$\mathcal P\in V\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^2V\otimes K_X$ and a Hermitian endomorphism
$Q$ of $V\otimes K_X$ such that, in a unitary frame,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:decomp}
\begin{split}
R_{i\bar j k\bar l}={}&\frac c2(\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{il}\delta_{kj})
+\varepsilon_{ika}\mathcal P^{a,jl}+\varepsilon_{jlb}\overline{\mathcal P^{b,ik}}
+\varepsilon_{ika}\varepsilon_{jlb}Q_{ab}.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
For $c\ne0$, $\mathcal P=c\mathsf P$, where
$P_{ik}^{jl}=\varepsilon_{ika}\mathsf P^{a,jl}$. At $c=0$ the tensor
$\mathcal P$ is defined directly by this decomposition, with no division by $c$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Split the two index pairs into their symmetric and alternating parts.
Polarization \eqref{p:eq:HSC} fixes the symmetric--symmetric part.
The parallel isomorphism $\Lambda^2V^*\simeq V\otimes K_X$
encodes the alternating--symmetric part by $\mathcal P$.
Hermitian symmetry determines the symmetric--alternating part as its
conjugate and makes the double-alternating encoding Hermitian.
The four symmetry projections are complementary, proving uniqueness.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{auto-sing:local-alternative}
At every point of a Hermitian threefold with constant Chern HSC $c\ne0$,
\[
 A_x\ne0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathscr K_x\ne0.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:general-curvature-transport}
On a Hermitian manifold with constant Chern HSC $c\ne0$, the tensor $P$
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{hd-full-F}
\begin{aligned}
 \nabla_pP_{ik}^{jl}={}&\tfrac14(
 T^j{}_{ip}\delta_k^l+T^l{}_{ip}\delta_k^j
 +T^j{}_{ik}\delta_p^l+T^l{}_{ik}\delta_p^j
 +T^j{}_{pk}\delta_i^l+T^l{}_{pk}\delta_i^j)\\
 &+\tfrac12(T^r{}_{ip}P_{rk}^{jl}
          +T^r{}_{ik}P_{rp}^{jl}+T^r{}_{pk}P_{ri}^{jl}).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
No condition on the common-curvature kernel is required.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Extend all arguments parallel at a point and fix $\bar Y$. Put
$r(U,W)=R(U,\bar Y,W,\bar Y)$ and
$d_{pik}=(\nabla_pR)_{i\bar Y k\bar Y}$.
Differentiated polarization gives $d_{pik}=-d_{pki}$, and second
Bianchi gives
$d_{pik}-d_{ipk}=r(T(e_i,e_p),e_k)$.
Using the three differences in the identity
\[
 2d_{pik}=(d_{pik}-d_{ipk})-(d_{ikp}-d_{kip})
                         +(d_{kpi}-d_{pki})
\]
and polarizing the barred arguments yields
\begin{equation}\label{hd-Bianchi-inversion}
 (\nabla_p\mathcal R)_{ik}^{jl}
 =\tfrac12(T^r{}_{ip}\mathcal R_{rk}^{jl}
          +T^r{}_{ik}\mathcal R_{rp}^{jl}
          +T^r{}_{pk}\mathcal R_{ri}^{jl}).
\end{equation}
Substitute \eqref{hd-P-definition}. The space-form term is parallel,
and division by the nonzero constant $c$ gives \eqref{hd-full-F}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:biquadratic-all-n}
Let $W$ have dimension $n\ge2$, and let $F(w,z)$ be homogeneous of degree
two in each variable.  Put
\[
 F^\pm(w,z)=\tfrac12\{F(w,z)\pm F(z,w)\},\quad
 d_F(z)=F(z,z),\quad
 j_F(z)[u]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}F^-(z+tu,z)\right|_{t=0}.
\]
The two conditions $d_F=0$ and $j_F=0$ are equivalent to a unique
representation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:biquadratic-curvature}
 F(w,z)=\mathcal R(w,z,w,z),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal R$ is alternating in its first two and last two slots,
is unchanged by exchanging these pairs, and satisfies
\[
 \mathcal R(a,b,c,d)+\mathcal R(b,c,a,d)+\mathcal R(c,a,b,d)=0.
\]
More explicitly, write $F(w,z)=\mathcal T(w,w;z,z)$ by polarizing each
pair.  Under the two conditions above,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:biquadratic-explicit-recovery}
 \mathcal R(a,b,c,d)=\tfrac23\{
 \mathcal T(a,c;b,d)-\mathcal T(a,d;b,c)\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal T^-$ be the part antisymmetric under exchange of its pairs.
The condition $j_F=0$ says $\mathcal T^-(u,z;z,z)=0$.
Polarizing the three occurrences of $z$ gives
\[
 \mathcal T^-(u,v;x,y)+\mathcal T^-(u,x;v,y)
                   +\mathcal T^-(u,y;v,x)=0.
\]
Interchanging $u,v$ and adding cancels the last two terms by pair
exchange, so $\mathcal T^-=0$. Polarization of $F(z,z)=0$ now gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:biquadratic-three-pairings}
 \mathcal T(a,b;c,d)+\mathcal T(a,c;b,d)
                         +\mathcal T(a,d;b,c)=0.
\end{equation}
This verifies the claimed symmetries of the recovery formula; its
cyclic sum cancels term by term. Taking $a=c=w$, $b=d=z$ gives
$\mathcal T(w,z;w,z)=-F(w,z)/2$, hence
$\mathcal R(w,z,w,z)=F(w,z)$.
Conversely, polarization recovers
\[
 \mathcal T(a,b;c,d)=\tfrac12\{
 \mathcal R(a,c,b,d)+\mathcal R(a,d,b,c)\}.
\]
The symmetries and cyclic identity recover the same $\mathcal R$,
proving uniqueness and the converse.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:six-evaluations}
Suppose $F$ is exchange-symmetric, biquadratic on $\mathbb C^3$, and $F(z,z)=0$.
There is a unique symmetric matrix $\Sigma$ for which
\[
 F(w,z)+\tfrac12\Sigma(z\times w,z\times w)=0.
\]
Set $q_0=F(e_1,e_2)$, $q_1=F(e_2,e_0)$ and $q_2=F(e_0,e_1)$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:six-evaluations}
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma_{ii}&=-2q_i\quad(0\le i\le2),\qquad \Sigma_{01}=q_0+q_1-F(e_0-e_1,e_2),\\
\Sigma_{02}&=q_0+q_2-F(e_2-e_0,e_1),\qquad \Sigma_{12}=q_1+q_2-F(e_1-e_2,e_0).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Existence and uniqueness follow from the preceding lemma and
$\Lambda^4\mathbb C^3=0$.  The first three evaluations give the diagonal
entries.  The other three cross products are $e_0+e_1$, $e_0+e_2$ and
$e_1+e_2$, respectively; subtract the already known diagonal terms.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:fund-compression}
For every symmetric $A$ and every $\mathsf P$, with $(q,p)=(1,2),(2,0),(0,1)$ indexed by $k=0,1,2$, the full system
\[
F_p^{a,bd}(D_q,\mathsf P)-F_q^{a,bd}(D_p,\mathsf P)+\tfrac32 A^{ka}Z^{bd}=0,
\quad \sum_pD_p^{pb}=0,\quad Z=Z^{\mathsf T},
\]
is naturally equivalent to the polynomial system
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fund-compression}
{B}(z)V(z)=3{q}(z)Zz,\qquad Z=Z^{\mathsf T}.
\end{equation}
Here $D$ is the unknown triple of matrices, $Z$ is an unknown symmetric
matrix, and $V$ is an unknown vector of quadratic polynomials.
For fixed $A,\mathsf P$, this correspondence is a bijection between the
two solution spaces: every polynomial solution $(V,Z)$ determines a
unique $D$ by \eqref{eq:fund-recovery}, the six-value recovery formula,
and \eqref{eq:fund-Dsplit}.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Let $v=z\times w$ and denote the linear difference of the two $F$ terms
by $\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf P}D$. Substituting \eqref{eq:fund-Dsplit} gives
\[
(\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf P}D)(w,w;z,z)
=-\mathbf p(z)\cdot V(w)+\sum_{p,a,b}z_av^pE_p^{ab}w_b+\tfrac12{\mathsf H_{\rm rec}}(v,v).
\]
The first index pair and the second pair are each symmetric. Put
\[
\mathcal Q(w,z)=(\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf P}D)(w,w;z,z)+\tfrac32{q}(w)z^{\mathsf T}Zz,
\]
and let $\mathcal Q_a(w,z)=(\mathcal Q(w,z)-\mathcal Q(z,w))/2$ and
$\mathcal Q_\Delta(z)=\mathcal Q(z,z)$. Direct differentiation of the
displayed polynomial gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fund-compression-identity}
{B} V-3{q} Zz=-\tfrac12\partial_z\mathcal Q_\Delta
+\left.\partial_w\mathcal Q_a(w,z)\right|_{w=z}.
\end{equation}
The ${\mathsf H_{\rm rec}}$ term has zero diagonal and first diagonal derivative.
Put $j_{\mathcal Q}(z)=\left.\partial_w\mathcal Q_a(w,z)\right|_{w=z}$.
Since $\mathcal Q_a$ is biquadratic and $\mathcal Q_a(z,z)=0$,
Euler's identity gives $z\cdot j_{\mathcal Q}=2\mathcal Q_a(z,z)=0$,
whereas $z\cdot\partial_z\mathcal Q_\Delta=4\mathcal Q_\Delta$.
If $BV=3qZz$, contraction with $z$ in \eqref{eq:fund-compression-identity}
first gives $-2\mathcal Q_\Delta=0$, hence
$\mathcal Q_\Delta=0$, then the first diagonal derivative of
$\mathcal Q_a$ vanishes. With ${\mathsf H_{\rm rec}}=0$, the polarization lemma and
Corollary~\ref{cor:six-evaluations} therefore give the unique ${\mathsf H_{\rm rec}}$
canceling the residual. Equations \eqref{eq:fund-recovery} and
\eqref{eq:fund-Dsplit} recover $D$. The converse follows from
\eqref{eq:fund-compression-identity}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{alg14:recurrence}
Let $U$ be an open subset of a Hermitian threefold with $H_h\equiv c\ne0$.
If $\mathcal D=0$ and $G=0$ on $U$, then $A=0$ on $U$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Suppose $A$ is nonzero at some point of $U$. Restrict to a nonempty
neighborhood on which $A\ne0$. Since $\mathcal D=0$, the connection
equation on this neighborhood is
\[
 \nabla'_pC=\mathcal H_p(C)
    =T_pC-CT_p^{\mathsf T}+\eta_pC.
\]
Its pure commutator is
\[
 \mathcal K^{a,bl}
 =(2C^{ab}+C^{ba})j^l-C^{al}j^b+C^{bl}j^a
      +2\det(C)\varepsilon_{abl},\qquad j=-C\eta=-A\eta.
\]
For the cycles \((q,p)=(1,2),(2,0),(0,1)\), indexed by \(a\),
the left side is
\(D\mathcal H_p[\mathcal H_q]-D\mathcal H_q[\mathcal H_p]
+T^r_{qp}\mathcal H_r\); it vanishes by the Chern
\((2,0)\) commutator.  Its full derivative is
\[
 D\mathcal H_p[Z]=T_p(Z)C+T_p(C)Z-ZT_p(C)^{\mathsf T}
 -CT_p(Z)^{\mathsf T}+\eta_p(Z)C+\eta_p(C)Z .
\]
Substitution gives the cubic formula. Symmetrizing \(a,b\) yields \(6A^{ab}j^l=0\).
As \(A\ne0\), it follows that \(j=0\) and then \(\det C=0\).
Moreover \(G=0\) and \(A\ne0\) imply \(\eta\ne0\).
The left and right null equations \(C\eta=C^{\mathsf T}\eta=0\)
give
\[
 \operatorname{adj}C=\kappa\eta\eta^{\mathsf T}
\]
locally: a frame putting the nonzero
covector \(\eta\) along the first coordinate makes the first row
and column of \(C\) zero, so only one cofactor can remain.
Using \eqref{eq:fund-Hsym}--\eqref{eq:fund-etaH},
differentiate $G=A-\eta_a\mathsf P^a=0$. Since $j=0$, this gives
\[
 0=\nabla'_pG=4(\operatorname{adj}C)_{pa}\mathsf P^a
   +\tfrac52\eta_pG=4\kappa\eta_pA.
\]
Hence \(\kappa=0\), so \(\operatorname{adj}C=0\).
The nonzero matrix \(C\) therefore has rank one on the whole open
set.  The identity
\[
 \mathcal H_p(vu^{\mathsf T})=2\eta_p(vu^{\mathsf T})
\]
follows from \(T_pC=0\) and \(CT_p^{\mathsf T}=-\eta_pC\).
Consequently \(\nabla'_pC=2\eta_pC\).


The mixed Chern equation excludes the remaining rank-one state.
Symmetrizing this equation in
its two output slots cancels the undetermined $\nabla Q$ terms while
retaining the curvature action on both vector slots and $K_X$.
In a unitary frame at a single point, write
$C=\varrho e_0\otimes(ae_0+e_2)$ with $\varrho>0$ and $a\ge0$.
The mixed equations and the barred tangent equations of the rank-one
locus have the two residual combinations
\[
\mathscr E_1=a^2c=0,\qquad \mathscr E_2=7c+a\mathscr K_1=0.
\]
Their complete equations, ordering, and coefficients are given in
Appendix~\ref{app:recurrent-certificate}. The scale is divided out
only after differentiating; no derivative of $\varrho$ is set to zero.
Since $c\ne0$, the first identity gives $a=0$, and the second is then
impossible. Thus $A$ vanishes throughout $U$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{alg14:coprime}
There is no nonempty open set with $c\ne0$, $q\ne0$, $\Delta\ne0$,
and $\gcd(q,\Delta)=1$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Multiplying $BW_{\mathrm{src}}=3qC^{\mathsf T}z$ by $J$ shows that $q$ divides $W_{\mathrm{src}}$.
Write $W_{\mathrm{src}}=3qv$. Then $Bv=C^{\mathsf T}z$.
The coefficient matrix of $D \mathbf p^{\mathsf T}v$ is symmetric;
the skew part of this equation gives $v=\eta/2$.
Thus $V=0$ and $G=0$, and exact recovery gives $\mathcal D=0$.
Proposition~\ref{alg14:recurrence} supplies the contradiction.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{r17:rank-one-entry}
Let $\dim_{\mathbb C}X=3$ and $c\ne0$. Suppose that on an open set there
are smooth $u,\xi$ with $u\ne0$, $\xi(u)=1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{r17:cut}
 P(u,x)=-\tfrac12u\odot x+\xi(x)u^2\qquad(x\in V).
\end{equation}
Then, for $L_{\mathrm{cut}}=\mathbb Cu$,
\[
 \nabla'L_{\mathrm{cut}}\subset L_{\mathrm{cut}},\qquad T(V,V)\subset L_{\mathrm{cut}}.
\]
On the open subset where $T\ne0$, the equations further give
\[
 T=-\eta\wedge(u\otimes\xi),\quad\eta(u)=0,\quad\eta\ne0,
 \qquad \operatorname{im}P\subset L_{\mathrm{cut}}\odot V.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Work on the stated open set, and put $v_p=\nabla_pu$ and
$\pi:V\to V/L_{\mathrm{cut}}$. Differentiating the cut gives
\begin{equation}\label{r17:cut-derivative}
 F_p(u,x)+P(v_p,x)
 =-\tfrac12v_p\odot x+(\nabla_p\xi)(x)u^2+\xi(x)u\odot v_p.
\end{equation}
If $\pi^2F_p(u,x)=0$, evaluation of its projection at $x=v_p$
shows $\pi(v_p)^2=0$. Hence $v_p\in L_{\mathrm{cut}}$, and substitution back shows
that $F_p(u,x)$ is a multiple of $u^2$. For $p=u$, the full transport is
\[
 F_u(u,x)=u\odot T(u,x)-\xi(T(u,x))u^2.
\]
It follows first that $T(u,x)=a(x)u$, with $a(u)=0$. For arbitrary $p$,
substitution of this conclusion into the same transport gives
\begin{equation}\label{r17:second-entry-identity}
 F_p(u,x)=\tfrac12u\odot T(p,x)
 +\tfrac12\{a(p)\xi(x)+a(x)\xi(p)-\xi(T(p,x))\}u^2.
\end{equation}
Its projected output again vanishes. The preceding implication now
proves both $\nabla'L_{\mathrm{cut}}\subset L_{\mathrm{cut}}$ and $T(V,V)\subset L_{\mathrm{cut}}$.

Write $T=u\alpha$. The complete transport becomes
\begin{equation}\label{alg16:cut-F}
 F_p(x,y)=\tfrac12\{\alpha(x,p)\xi(y)+\alpha(x,y)\xi(p)
                              +\alpha(p,y)\xi(x)\}u^2.
\end{equation}
For $p,q\in\ker\xi$, the pure commutator
\eqref{eq:pure-main}, evaluated on $(p,q)$, has zero derivative terms
and three remaining terms each equal to $\alpha(p,q)^2u^2/2$.
Thus $\alpha|_{\Lambda^2\ker\xi}=0$. Since
$\eta(x)=\alpha(u,x)$, this is
$\alpha=-\eta\wedge\xi$, with $\eta(u)=0$.
No nonzero scalar has been canceled except a chosen nonzero component
of $u$; where $T\ne0$, necessarily $\eta\ne0$.

Finally, in a barred derivative the output of $\nabla T$ modulo $L_{\mathrm{cut}}$
is $\alpha(x,y)\pi(\nabla''u)$. The barred-symmetric first Bianchi
identity therefore has the form
$\pi^2P(x,y)=\alpha(x,y)B$ for a single
$B\in\operatorname{Sym}^2(V/L_{\mathrm{cut}})$. The cut gives $\pi^2P(u,x)=0$, and
$\alpha(u,x)=\eta(x)\ne0$ for some $x$ on the torsion-nonzero locus.
Hence $B=0$ there, proving the asserted output support.
Appendix~\ref{calc:r17:rank-one-entry} records the individual contractions.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{geo16:partial-transport}
Set $\alpha=-\eta\wedge\xi$, so $T=u\alpha$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{geo16:rank-one-F}
 \nabla_pP(x,y)=\xi(p)\alpha(x,y)u^2
 =\tfrac12\bigl((\Pi p)\odot T(x,y)\bigr).
\end{equation}
There is a covector $\zeta$, with $\zeta(u)=0$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{geo16:partial-derivatives}
 \nabla_p\Pi=(\Pi p)\otimes\eta,\qquad
 \nabla_p\eta=2\eta(p)\eta-\xi(p)\zeta.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Substitute $\alpha=-\eta\wedge\xi$ in \eqref{alg16:cut-F}.
Writing $\nabla_pu=\lambda_pu$, differentiate the cut; its $u^2$
coefficient gives
\[
 \nabla_p\xi=-\lambda_p\xi+\xi(p)\eta,
\]
which proves the projector equation. The $(2,0)$ commutator
\[
 (\nabla^2_{p,q}-\nabla^2_{q,p})\Pi=-\nabla_{T(p,q)}\Pi
\]
then gives
\[
 \xi(p)\{\nabla_q\eta-2\eta(q)\eta\}
 -\xi(q)\{\nabla_p\eta-2\eta(p)\eta\}=0.
\]
This is the second equation; differentiating $\eta(u)=0$ gives
$\zeta(u)=0$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{geo16:orthogonal-all-n}
On a threefold with $c\ne0$, no nonempty open set can satisfy
\eqref{geo16:partial-input} and
\begin{equation}\label{geo16:orthogonality}
T(L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp,L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp)=0 .
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Work on the open set in the statement. Choose $u$ unit and write
$H=L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp$ and $\nu=\langle\,\cdot\,,u\rangle_h$. Metric compatibility gives
$\nabla''H\subset H$. Differentiate $T(H,H)=0$ there before making
any pointwise frame choice. The two differentiated inputs stay in $H$,
