so first Bianchi gives
\begin{equation}\label{geo16:HHzero}
 P(H,H)=0.
\end{equation}

For a $(1,0)$ direction $p$, set
$\mu_p(x)=\nu(\nabla_px)$ for $x\in H$. Differentiate $P(H,H)=0$
using \eqref{geo16:rank-one-F}. Modulo $\operatorname{Sym}^2L_{\mathrm{cut}}$ the result is
\[
 0=\tfrac12u\odot\{\mu_p(x)y-\mu_p(y)x\}\qquad(x,y\in H).
\]
The map $x\mapsto u\odot x$ is injective on $H$; because $\dim H=2$,
this forces $\mu_p=0$. Thus $\nabla'H\subset H$, and metric adjoints
show that $L_{\mathrm{cut}}\oplus H$ is fully Chern parallel on this neighborhood.

Curvature consequently preserves the splitting. For $x\in H$,
\[
 0=R(u,\bar u,x,\bar u)=cP(u,x)(\nu,\nu)=c\xi(x).
\]
The alternating barred curvature vanishes here because the barred
arguments repeat. Since $c\ne0$, $\xi=\nu$. Together with $P(H,H)=0$
and the cut, this implies $P(x,y)(\nu,\nu)=0$ for all $x,y$.
The covector line $\mathbb C\nu$ is parallel, so its full differentiated
contraction also vanishes. But \eqref{geo16:rank-one-F}, with
$p=x=u$ and $y\in H$, now gives
\[
 0=(\nabla_uP)(u,y)(\nu,\nu)=\eta(y).
\]
Together with $\eta(u)=0$, this contradicts $T\ne0$.
The connection-slot computation is given in
Appendix~\ref{calc:geo16:orthogonal-all-n}.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{geo13:nonorthogonal-main}
On a Hermitian threefold with $c\ne0$, no nonempty open set can satisfy
\eqref{geo16:partial-input} and $T(L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp,L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp)\ne0$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Restrict to the nonorthogonal open set and then to a smaller chart.
If the coefficient represented below by $r$ is nonzero somewhere,
shrink to its nonzero locus and choose its phase; otherwise it
vanishes identically. Thus it suffices to consider smooth unitary
charts of the form
\begin{equation}\label{geo13:chart}
 u=e_0,\qquad \xi=e^0+se^1,\qquad
 \eta=-re^1-te^2,\qquad s,t>0,
\end{equation}
with either $r>0$ or $r\equiv0$.
No smooth phase choice through an arbitrary zero is needed.
The torsion and curvature
support determine the family \eqref{geo13:chart-tensors}; its three
initially complex coefficients are
$A_{\mathrm{cut}},B_{\mathrm{cut}},C_{\mathrm{cut}}$.
The barred first Bianchi equation, including the Hermitian condition
$Q=Q^*$, gives
\[
 B_{\mathrm{cut}}=r\delta,\qquad C_{\mathrm{cut}}=t\delta,
 \qquad \delta\in\mathbb R.
\]
These are identities on the chart. They do not set the connection
coefficients to zero: only $(\Gamma_p)_{10}=(\Gamma_p)_{20}=0$
is imposed by $\nabla'L_{\mathrm{cut}}\subset L_{\mathrm{cut}}$, and
$\Gamma_{\bar p}=-\Gamma_p^*$.

The further restriction comes from both the first and barred equations.
For the unit-line factorization $C=v\otimes u$ and $\mathbf p(z)=u(z)Lz$, put
\begin{equation}\label{geo13:invariant-beta}
 w=\langle v,u\rangle,\quad k=-\langle L\eta,u\rangle,
 \quad\varrho^2=|\eta|^2,\quad\beta=\overline w k.
\end{equation}
The quantities $w$ and $k$ are coefficients in a unitary canonical-line
frame. The phases of that frame and of $u$ cancel in
$\beta,|w|^2,\varrho^2$. The two residual identities
\eqref{geo13:two-source-identities} give
\begin{equation}\label{geo13:state-polynomial}
 \beta\in\mathbb R,\qquad
 \beta(\beta+2|w|^2+3\varrho^2)=0.
\end{equation}
They are formed from the full residuals \eqref{geo13:residuals}, with
all nine real entries of $Q$, every allowed connection entry, and all
moduli derivatives retained. In the alternative chart used to obtain
these identities, the only divisions are by the positive scale,
the nonzero nonorthogonality parameter, and $c$; the scale is divided
out after differentiation, so its derivative is still free.

In the present chart, $w=-st$, $k=2\delta(r^2+t^2)$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{geo13:LKJ}
 \mathsf L_{\mathrm{cut}}=r^2+t^2,\quad
 K_{\mathrm{cut}}=s^2t^2+\mathsf L_{\mathrm{cut}},\quad
 J_{\mathrm{cut}}=2s^2t^2+3\mathsf L_{\mathrm{cut}}.
\end{equation}
The state equation has exactly the two roots
\begin{equation}\label{geo13:two-roots}
 \delta=0,\qquad
 \delta=\frac{J_{\mathrm{cut}}}{2st\mathsf L_{\mathrm{cut}}}.
\end{equation}
Their separation is strict because $s,t,\mathsf L_{\mathrm{cut}},J_{\mathrm{cut}}>0$.
After shrinking around any point, one selected root is therefore an
identity on the neighborhood. Only now do we differentiate its formulas
for $B_{\mathrm{cut}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{cut}}$.

For the zero root these coefficients and their derivatives vanish.
The twelve first/barred identities \eqref{geo13:zero-twelve}, whose
only denominators are $t$, $t^2$, and $st$, give
$(\Gamma_p)_{01}=(\Gamma_p)_{02}=0$ for every $p$.
Together with recurrence and metric adjoints, this makes
$L_{\mathrm{cut}}\oplus L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp$ fully Chern parallel. It is essential here to obtain
parallelism on a neighborhood, not merely zeros at a point.
Curvature preservation would then force
\begin{equation}\label{geo13:mixed-endpoint}
 0=R_{0\bar0\,1\bar0}=cP_{01}^{00}=cs,
\end{equation}
which is impossible.

For the other root, use its differentiated rational formulas and let
$R_j$ be the real residuals ordered in \eqref{geo13:residual-order},
with the derivative and Riccati rows
\eqref{geo13:derivative-rows}--\eqref{geo13:Riccati-rows} appended.
The identities with the multipliers listed in
Appendix~\ref{geo13:nonzero-root} are
\[
 \sum_{j\in\mathcal J}m_jR_j
       =-18cr\mathsf L_{\mathrm{cut}}^2K_{\mathrm{cut}},
\]
and, at $r=0$,
\[
 2s^3t(R_{38}-R_{48}-R_{86})
 -3s(R_{56}+R_{72})-3s^2(R_{59}+R_{75})
 =-18c(s^2+1).
\]
All residuals vanish for a geometric solution. If $r\ne0$, the first
right side is nonzero; if $r=0$, the second is nonzero. In the second
identity the family is differentiated before setting $r=0$, so no
moving-frame or parameter derivative has been discarded. The only
rational denominators in this branch are products of $s,t$ and
$\mathsf L_{\mathrm{cut}}$, all nonzero. Both roots are excluded.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{r17:no-rank-one-cut}
Let a Hermitian threefold have constant Chern holomorphic sectional
curvature $c\ne0$.  There is no nonempty open set carrying
smooth $u\ne0,\xi$ with $\xi(u)=1$ and
\[
 P(u,x)=-\tfrac12u\odot x+\xi(x)u^2\qquad(x\in V).
\]
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
On the open subset where $T\ne0$, Theorem~\ref{r17:rank-one-entry}
supplies the line support and projector identities on the open set.
If $T(L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp,L_{\mathrm{cut}}^\perp)$ is nonzero at any point, it is nonzero
on a smaller open set, contrary to Theorem~\ref{geo13:nonorthogonal-main}.
It therefore vanishes identically on this torsion-nonzero open set,
which is ruled out by Theorem~\ref{geo16:orthogonal-all-n}.
Hence $T=0$ throughout the original open set.  Its barred derivative
then vanishes, so \eqref{b:eq:P-torsion} gives $P=0$ there.
The cut is nonzero for any $x$ independent of $u$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-factor-charts}
Every nonempty open set with \(q\ne0\) and \(\Delta\ne0\)
contains a nonempty smaller open set on which the rank of \(A\),
the degree of \(\gcd(q,\Delta)\), and the multiplicities of the
selected linear factors in \(\Delta\) are constant. On this set the
factors and polynomial quotients used below can be chosen smoothly.
A repeated quadratic is written \(q=\kappa\ell^2\), with
\(\kappa\ne0\); its scale and its derivatives are retained.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
First restrict to a constant-rank chart of \(A\). A rank-three
quadratic is irreducible, so its gcd with \(\Delta\) has degree zero
or two. A rank-two quadratic has two distinct projective linear
factors, which admit a smooth local ordering. For rank one, choose
\(A_{ii}\ne0\), set
\(\ell=z_i+\sum_{j\ne i}(A_{ij}/A_{ii})z_j\), and take
\(\kappa=A_{ii}\). This retains the nonzero scale.
Divisibility by \(q\) or its selected factors, and factor multiplicities
at most three in \(\Delta\), are finite closed coefficient conditions.
Restrict successively to a nonempty open part where each condition
holds identically or fails; this fixes the gcd degree and multiplicities.
Polynomial division is a linear coefficient system, and a nonzero
maximal minor gives its smooth quotient. Thus every nonempty open set under consideration contains a required
chart. This suffices for the open-set exclusion; the pointwise result
follows from openness of a nonzero coefficient and is proved at the
end of the section.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{quot14:radial-endpoint}
There is no open set with \(q\ne0\), \(\Delta\ne0\), and
\[
 \mathbf p=2\rho Az-qr,\qquad \rho=r^{\mathsf T}z,\qquad
 \Delta=q\ell,\quad \ell\mid\mathfrak r.
\]
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Work on the stated open set and retain $\rho=r^{\mathsf T}z$ as a
polynomial. The symmetric-plus-skew adjugate formula gives
\[
 D=1+4r^{\mathsf T}(\operatorname{adj}A)r,\quad
 \Delta=2Dq\rho,\quad \mathfrak r=Dq+\rho\,b(z),
\]
where the quadratic trace expansion specifies the linear $b(z)$ in
\eqref{quot14:radial-trace}. Since $\Delta\ne0$, both $D$ and $\rho$
are nonzero, and $\ell=2D\rho$. Thus $\ell\mid\mathfrak r$ implies
$\rho\mid q$. Write $q=\rho m$, $m=s^{\mathsf T}z$; then $\mathbf p=s\rho^2$.
Restricting its full first transport to $\rho=0$ gives
$C(\ker\rho)=0$, hence $C=sr^{\mathsf T}$ and $\eta=s\times r$.
After canceling the nonzero polynomial $\rho$, the transport reads
\[
 \rho\nabla_i s+2s\nabla_i\rho
   =s z_i-\tfrac12e_i m+\eta_i s\rho.
\]
Project to $V/\mathbb Cs$ and restrict to $\rho=0$. Some $e_i$ has a
nonzero quotient class, so $m|_{\rho=0}=0$. Consequently
$s=\varrho r$ with $\varrho\ne0$ on a smaller chart, and
$C=\varrho rr^{\mathsf T}$, $\eta=0$,
$\mathsf P^{a,jl}=\varrho r_ar_jr_l$.
The last tensor is totally symmetric on the whole chart, including
its canonical-line factor. Its covariant derivative must preserve
that symmetry. But its prescribed transport satisfies
\[
 F_i^{a,jl}-F_i^{j,al}
       =\varrho(r_a\delta_i^j-r_j\delta_i^a)r_l\ne0
\]
for suitable indices, since $r\ne0$ and $\varrho\ne0$.
This is the contradiction. The adjugate coefficients are recorded in
Appendix~\ref{calc:quot14:radial-endpoint}.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{quot14:reduction}
On an open subset of a Hermitian threefold with constant Chern HSC \(c\ne0\),
suppose \(q\ne0\) and \(\Delta=q\ell\ne0\).  After restriction to
the nonempty coefficient charts needed below, every surviving state
has a linear-source presentation
\[
 q=a m,\qquad W_{\mathrm{src}}=a{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z,\qquad B{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z=3mC^{\mathsf T}z,
 \qquad {\mathsf H_{\rm src}}=I+b\otimes m.
\]
Here \(a,m\) are nonzero linear polynomials and may coincide.
In particular $\operatorname{rank}{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}\ge2$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Differentiate $\Delta=q\ell$ on the coefficient chart, rather than
at an isolated normalized point. Exact source recovery and determinant
transport give \eqref{quot14:jet}. On each multiplicity chart
$q=\ell^kh$ ($k=0,1,2$), comparison on $\ker\ell$ gives
\[
 \mathfrak r=\ell r_1,\qquad
 \nabla_i\ell=\varrho z_i+u_i\ell,
 \qquad \varrho=0\quad\hbox{if }\ell\nmid q.
\]
For $k=1,2$ the transverse leading factors are respectively $7h$ and
$11h$, nonzero on the plane; for $k=0$ a nonzero $\varrho$ would force
$\ell\mid q$ by the pure commutator. Thus all multiplicities are
covered, as expanded in \eqref{quot14:multiplicity}.
Substitution into the source gives
\[
 V=za+qv,
\]
with a linear polynomial $a$ and a covector $v$;
$V$ carries the derivative covector slot, just as the formal covector $z$ does; the formulas are
\eqref{quot14:radial-V}.

There are three possibilities on a smaller nonempty open chart.
If $a=0$, then $Bv=3Gz$; its skew part gives $v=0$, then $G=0$, and
exact compression gives $\mathcal D=0$. The recurrent obstruction
excludes this case. If $a\ne0$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$, then $q\mid Bz$.
Euler's formula gives $\mathbf p=2\rho Az-qr$, with $\rho=r^{\mathsf T}z$,
which is precisely the radial endpoint just excluded.
The remaining case is $a\mid q$; write $q=am$. Then
\[
 W_{\mathrm{src}}=a\{z+m(v+\tfrac32\eta)\}=a{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z.
\]
Canceling the nonzero polynomial $a$ in $BW_{\mathrm{src}}=3qC^{\mathsf T}z$ gives
the asserted linear source. This is cancellation in the polynomial
ring; no assertion that a chosen covector lies off its zero set is
needed. Appendix~\ref{calc:quot14:reduction} supplies the coefficient
expressions used in the factor comparison.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{alg14:linear-source}
On an open subset of a Hermitian threefold with constant Chern HSC $c\ne0$, suppose
\[
 q=\ell m\ne0,\quad\Delta\not\equiv0,\quad \ell\mid\Delta,\quad
 B{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z=3\ell C^{\mathsf T}z,\quad W_{\mathrm{src}}=m{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z .
\]
Choose smooth factor charts and exact multiplicity charts for the
chosen factor of \(\Delta\).  The factors may coincide.
Then
\[
 {\mathsf H_{\rm src}}=\lambda I+v a^{\mathsf T},\qquad \ell=a^{\mathsf T}z.
\]
The scalar \(\lambda\) cannot vanish on a nonempty open subregion.
Rescaling the factors where $\lambda\ne0$, set
\({\mathsf H_{\rm src}}=I+v a^{\mathsf T}\).  On this chart put
\(\delta=1+a\cdot v\).  Every point with \(\delta=0\) is excluded
by the regular-pencil hypothesis.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Fix an exact multiplicity chart $\Delta=\ell^kR$, where
$1\le k\le3$ and $R|_{\ker\ell}\not\equiv0$.
The quadratic jet obtained from source recovery and the determinant
transport give, respectively for distinct and repeated factors,
\[
 (k+\tfrac13)R({\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z\wedge z)=0,
 \qquad(\tfrac k2+\tfrac13)R({\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z\wedge z)=0
 \quad\hbox{on }\ker\ell.
\]
The scalar multipliers and the polynomial $R|_{\ker\ell}$ are nonzero.
Cancellation in the coordinate ring of the plane therefore shows
that the source map preserves every line of this two-dimensional
plane. It is scalar on the plane, so
${\mathsf H_{\rm src}}=\lambda I+va^{\mathsf T}$.

If $\lambda$ vanishes on an open subregion, the source gives
$Bv=3C^{\mathsf T}z$. Its skew part forces $v=3\eta/2$, hence
$V=G=0$ and $\mathcal D=0$, contrary to the recurrent obstruction.
On the nonzero-$\lambda$ chart, rescale
$({\mathsf H_{\rm src}},\ell,m)$ to
$({\mathsf H_{\rm src}}/\lambda,\ell/\lambda,\lambda m)$.
With $b=v-3\eta/2$, polarization gives a scalar quadratic $h$ such that
\[
 \mathbf p=ah+\ell(b\times z),\qquad
 \delta h=\tfrac32\ell\{m+(v\times\eta)\cdot z\}.
\]
This identity was obtained without dividing by $\delta$.
If $\delta=0$ at a point, then $m=-v\times\eta$.
A repeated factor is impossible because $m(v)=0$ but $\ell(v)=-1$.
For distinct factors, differentiate the displayed open identity
before evaluating at that point. The normal factor jet and first
transport imply $C(\ker\ell)\subset\mathbb Ca$ and $a\cdot\eta=0$.
Thus $C=da^{\mathsf T}$ and $a\cdot b=-1$.
In a frame with $a=e_0$, the lower right $2\times2$ block of $B$ is
zero, so $\Delta\equiv0$, contradicting regularity.
Hence division by $\delta$ is allowed only after this exclusion.
The unreduced factor-jet and block calculations are in
Appendix~\ref{calc:alg14:linear-source}.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{alg14:distinct-closed}
There is no nonempty open subset of a Hermitian threefold with
constant Chern HSC $c\ne0$ on which the regular source satisfies
\[
 q=\ell m\ne0,\quad \ell,m\text{ independent},\quad
 B{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z=3\ell C^{\mathsf T}z,\quad \Delta\not\equiv0,\quad \ell\mid\Delta.
\]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Work on a smooth independent-factor chart, after the scalar-zero and
singular-source boundaries have been excluded. Write
$\ell=a^{\mathsf T}z$, $m=d^{\mathsf T}z$ and
${\mathsf H_{\rm src}}=I+va^{\mathsf T}$, with
$\delta=1+a\cdot v\ne0$.
Normal transport on $\ker\ell$ first excludes $\delta=-1$ and gives
the complete surviving family
\begin{equation}\label{alg14:distinct-family}
 C=da^{\mathsf T}-\frac{\delta}{3(\delta+1)}[v]_\times,
 \qquad
 \mathbf p(z)=\frac{\ell}{\delta+1}(v\times z)
 +\frac32\ell^2\left(d-\frac{v\cdot d}{\delta}a\right).
\end{equation}
Its determinant is
\begin{equation}\label{alg14:distinct-det}
 \Delta=\frac{6\delta}{\delta+1}\ell^2
       \left(m-\frac{v\cdot d}{\delta+1}\ell\right).
\end{equation}
Independence of $\ell,m$ makes the multiplicity of $\ell$ exactly two.
Comparing this multiplicity with the normal factor law
$\nabla_i\ell\equiv-\delta z_i/3\pmod\ell$ and determinant transport
gives the identity
\[
 \left.\frac{\delta(\delta+2)}{\delta+1}m\right|_{\ker\ell}=0.
\]
The factors $\delta$, $\delta+1$, and $m|_{\ker\ell}$ are all
nonzero in the senses already specified. Therefore $\delta=-2$
on the chart; this value is fixed before endpoint differentiation.
\begin{equation}\label{alg14:distinct-delta}
 \delta=-2.
\end{equation}

Differentiate the full displayed family, retaining all nine
covariant derivatives of $(a,d,v)$ in direction $e_2$. Only then
choose a determinant-one point frame with
$a=e_0$, $v=-3e^0$, $d=(\mu,1,0)^{\mathsf T}$, where $\mu$ is arbitrary.
Recover $X=\nabla'C$ from the exact source, and let
$\mathcal E_C=d_{\rm par}C-X_2$ and
$\mathcal E_{\mathsf P}=d_{\rm par}\mathsf P-F_2(C,\mathsf P)$.
These must vanish for a geometric solution, whereas
\[
 -\tfrac34\mathcal E_C^{01}+\mathcal E_C^{10}
 +\tfrac14\mathcal E_C^{12}-\tfrac14\mathcal E_C^{21}
 +\mathcal E_{\mathsf P}^{0,01}
 -\tfrac23\mathcal E_{\mathsf P}^{1,00}
 -\tfrac16\mathcal E_{\mathsf P}^{1,02}=-1.
\]
This contradiction holds for every $\mu$ and all retained derivatives.
The seven residual expansions and the normal-family calculation are
in Appendix~\ref{calc:alg14:distinct-closed}.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{geo14:repeated-closed}
There is no nonempty open subset of a constant nonzero Chern-HSC
threefold on the regular-pencil locus carrying the repeated
linear-source module
\eqref{geo14:linear-source-convention} together with its
quotient jet \eqref{geo14:ell-normal-jet}.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Keep the nonzero scale in $q=\kappa\ell^2$, with
$\ell=a^{\mathsf T}z$ and $\kappa\ne0$. The normal first transport,
together with the quotient jet, excludes $\delta=-1/2$ by an algebraic
contradiction and $\delta=1/4$ by $\Delta\equiv0$.
Together with the earlier exclusion $\delta=0$, these yield the
surviving family
\begin{equation}\label{geo14:repeated-normal-family}
 g(\delta)=\frac{2(1-2\delta)}{3(1+2\delta)},\quad
 \eta=-g(\delta)v,\quad
 C=\kappa aa^{\mathsf T}+\frac{g(\delta)}2[v]_\times,
 \qquad
 \mathbf p=\frac{3\kappa}{2\delta}a\ell^2
             +\frac{2}{1+2\delta}\ell[v]_\times z.
\end{equation}
Its determinant and adjugate trace are
$\Delta=\kappa D\ell^3$, $\mathfrak r=\kappa E\ell^2$, with
\[
 D=\frac{3(4\delta-1)^2}{\delta(2\delta+1)^2},\qquad
 E=\frac{(4\delta-1)(5\delta-2)}{\delta(2\delta+1)^2}.
\]
Differentiate the determinant before reducing modulo $\ell^3$.
The terms containing $\nabla\kappa$ and $\nabla\delta$ are multiples
of $\ell^3$; they are removed by the reduction, not set to zero.
After canceling the nonzero polynomial $\kappa\ell^2$, determinant
transport and the normal factor jet give
\[
 0=E-\frac{5-6\delta}{12}D
 =\frac{3(2\delta-1)(4\delta-1)(4\delta+1)}
          {4\delta(2\delta+1)^2}.
\]
The previously excluded values account for every canceled factor.
Thus $\delta=-1/4$ or $1/2$. On a connected smaller chart a root
is fixed, and only at this stage is $d\delta=0$ justified.

Differentiate the full family while retaining all seven covariant
derivatives of $(a,v,\kappa)$ in each direction, then normalize the
point frame to $a=e_0$, $v=(\delta-1)e^0$.
Let $\mathcal E_{i;a,jk}$ be the polynomial coefficient residual of
first transport, and let $\mathcal U$ be the pure tensor residual
\eqref{geo14:pure-slot-definition}. Their endpoint identities are
\[
 \delta=-\tfrac14:\qquad
 \mathcal E_{0;1,02}+24\nabla_0\delta=-\tfrac{15}{2},
\]
\[
 \delta=\tfrac12:\qquad
 \kappa(\mathcal E_{1;0,01}+\mathcal E_{1;1,00})
 +18\kappa^2\mathcal E_{2;1,22}-3\mathcal U_{12}^{0,00}
 =-\tfrac92\kappa^2.
\]
Every term on the left vanishes for a geometric solution; both right
sides are nonzero. This excludes both roots without normalizing away
$\kappa$ or its derivatives. Appendix~\ref{calc:geo14:repeated-closed}
contains the coefficient calculations and treats the two exceptional
normal families before any division by their factors.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{fin14:regular}
For a Hermitian threefold with constant Chern holomorphic sectional
curvature \(c\ne0\), there is no nonempty open set on which
\[
 A\ne0,\qquad \det B(z)\not\equiv0.
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Work on a nonempty coefficient chart from
Lemma~\ref{lem:local-factor-charts}. Multiplying the exact source
$BW_{\mathrm{src}}=3qC^{\mathsf T}z$ by $J=\operatorname{adj}B$ gives
\[
 \Delta W_{\mathrm{src}}=3qJC^{\mathsf T}z,
 \qquad (q/d)\mid W_{\mathrm{src}},\qquad d=\gcd(q,\Delta).
\]
The divisibility is componentwise in $\mathbb C[z_0,z_1,z_2]$:
$q/d$ and $\Delta/d$ are coprime, with multiplicities included.
For $\deg d=0$, Corollary~\ref{alg14:coprime} applies. For
$\deg d=1$, write $q=\ell m$, $d=\ell$. The quotient has the form
\[
 W_{\mathrm{src}}=m{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z,\qquad
 B{\mathsf H_{\rm src}}z=3\ell C^{\mathsf T}z,
\]
where ${\mathsf H_{\rm src}}$ is smooth and $\ell\mid\Delta$.
The linear-source results in the second row of the table exclude
this chart, including the scalar-zero and singular-source cases
treated in Theorem~\ref{alg14:linear-source}.

It remains to reduce degree two. Then $q\mid\Delta$, so
$\Delta=q\ell$ for a smooth nonzero linear polynomial $\ell$.
Proposition~\ref{quot14:reduction} excludes the recurrent and radial
endpoints and reduces every remaining open chart to a linear source
of the displayed form, after interchanging the factor names.
The selected factor still divides $\Delta$, because it divides $q$.
Thus the same linear-source exclusion applies, with its exact
multiplicity hypothesis satisfied.

These cases exhaust the gcd degrees. Every putative surviving open
set contains one of the coefficient charts just excluded, so no such
open set exists.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{auto-sing:nondegeneracy}
The pencil \(B\) has no nonzero constant right kernel, and
\[
 \sum_{i,j}\partial_{z_i}\partial_{z_j}J_{ij}=12.
\]
Its constant left kernel is the complete common-curvature kernel
\[
 \mathscr K
 =\{\nu\in V^*:2P(\cdot,\cdot)(\nu,w)=\nu\wedge w\text{ for every }w\in V^*\}.
\]
In particular, \(\Delta=0\) implies that \(B\) has rank exactly
two over the fraction field \(\mathbb C(z_0,z_1,z_2)\).
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
If \(Bt=0\) with \(t\) constant, then
\[
 \partial_z(t^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p)+[t]_\times z=0.
\]
The coefficient matrix of the first linear polynomial is a
symmetric Hessian, while \([t]_\times\) is skew-symmetric.
Both vanish, giving \(t=0\).

For the cofactor identity, write \(B=A_0+K\), where
\((A_0)_{ij}=\partial_i \mathbf p_j\) and
\(K_{ij}=\varepsilon_{ijk}z_k=-([z]_\times)_{ij}\).
The cofactor formula is
\[
 (\operatorname{adj}B)_{ij}
 =\frac12\varepsilon_{iab}\varepsilon_{jcd}B_{ca}B_{db}.
\]
Its double divergence is quadratic in the first derivatives of
\(A_0,K\), since both matrices are linear in \(z\).
The \(A_0A_0\) part vanishes by the Piola cancellation: commuting
the derivatives of \(\mathbf p\) pairs a symmetric derivative pair
with an alternating epsilon pair. In the two mixed terms the
epsilon contractions reduce to scalar multiples of
\(\varepsilon_{iab}\mathsf P^{a,bi}\) and
\(\varepsilon_{jcd}\mathsf P^{d,cj}\), respectively. They vanish by the
symmetry of the last two indices of \(\mathsf P^{a,kl}\).
Finally \(\operatorname{adj}K=zz^{\mathsf T}\), whose double
divergence is \(6+6=12\). This proves the identity and ensures
\(J\not\equiv0\).

The exact constant-left-kernel identity is
\[
 \varepsilon_{ija}(B(z)^{\mathsf T}\nu)_a
 =2P(e_i,e_j)(\nu,z)-(\nu_i z_j-\nu_j z_i).
\]
Indeed \(D_z\mathbf p\,\nu\) gives the first term, and
\(\varepsilon_{ija}([z]_\times\nu)_a
   =z_i\nu_j-z_j\nu_i\).
The epsilon identification is invertible, proving the claimed
equivalence. The last assertion now follows from
\(\det B=0\) and \(\operatorname{adj}B\ne0\).
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{auto-sing:adjugate-equations}
If \(\Delta(z)=0\) identically on an open set, then
\[
 \mathfrak r=0,\qquad JC^{\mathsf T}z=0
\]
on that open set.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Since $\Delta$ vanishes on the open set, determinant transport
\eqref{eq:fund-transport} gives $0=2z_i\mathfrak r-(JC^{\mathsf T}z)_i$.
Hence \(JC^{\mathsf T}z=2\mathfrak r z\).
Multiplying by \(B\) gives \(\mathfrak r Bz=0\).

If \(\mathfrak r\) were a nonzero polynomial at a point, the
polynomial domain would give \(Bz=0\) there.
For the cubic \(g=z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p\), Euler's identity gives
\[
 Bz=\partial_zg-\mathbf p,\qquad z^{\mathsf T}Bz=2g.
\]
Thus \(g=\mathbf p=0\), so \(B=-[z]_\times\), \(J=zz^{\mathsf T}\),
and \(\mathfrak r=z^{\mathsf T}C^{\mathsf T}z=z^{\mathsf T}Az\).
But \(JC^{\mathsf T}z=2\mathfrak r z\) now says
\(\mathfrak r z=2\mathfrak r z\), contradicting
\(\mathfrak r\ne0\).
Therefore \(\mathfrak r=0\), proving both equations.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{auto-sing:linear-syzygy}
At a point with \(\Delta=0\) and \(\mathscr K=0\), there are
matrices \(U,N\), both of rank at least two, such that
\[
 J(z)=(Uz)(Nz)^{\mathsf T},\qquad B(z)Uz=0.
\]
The space of homogeneous linear right syzygies \(B(z)Vz=0\)
is one-dimensional. On an open set satisfying these hypotheses,
every point has a neighborhood on which \(U\) can be chosen smoothly
and nowhere zero.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
The nonzero quadratic matrix \(J\) has fraction-field rank one.
Factor out the greatest common divisor of the entries of a
nonzero column and then those of a row. Unique factorization
in \(\mathbb C[z_0,z_1,z_2]\) gives
\[
 J=g(z)a(z)b(z)^{\mathsf T},
\]
with primitive homogeneous polynomial vectors \(a,b\).
Indeed, a denominator in a rational multiplier of a primitive
polynomial vector would divide every component; thus the column and
row multipliers are polynomial.

The equation \(BJ=0\) makes \(a\) a right syzygy. It cannot have
degree zero, by Lemma~\ref{auto-sing:nondegeneracy}.
Likewise \(JB=0\) and \(\mathscr K=0\) exclude degree zero
for \(b\). Their degrees sum to at most two, so both are linear
and \(g\) is a nonzero scalar, which can be absorbed into \(b\).
Write \(a=Uz\), \(b=Nz\). A primitive linear vector cannot have
coefficient rank one, since its entries would share a linear
factor; hence both ranks are at least two.

Over the fraction field, every right syzygy is a rational
multiple of \(Uz\). If \(Vz\) is another linear syzygy, primitivity
makes this multiplier polynomial; homogeneity makes it constant.
Thus the coefficient map
\[
 \operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^3)\longrightarrow
       \mathbb C^3\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathbb C^3)^*,
 \qquad V\longmapsto B(z)Vz
\]
has a one-dimensional kernel at every point of the stated open
set. Its coefficients depend smoothly on the base point. At a chosen point,
fix a nonzero rank-eight minor and shrink the neighborhood so that
this minor remains nonzero. Normalizing the remaining free coefficient
to one and solving these eight equations gives a smooth nowhere-zero
generator \(U\); the other equations hold because the kernel has
dimension one throughout this neighborhood.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{auto-sing:invertible-U}
Suppose \(\Delta=0\), \(\mathscr K=0\),
\(\mathfrak r=0\), \(JC^{\mathsf T}z=0\), and \(B(z)Uz=0\)
with \(U\) invertible. Then \(A=0\).
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
The following calculation initially requires no invertibility.
Put \(g=\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}Uz\). The syzygy equation gives
\[
 \partial_zg=z\times Uz+U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p.
\]
Contracting with \(z\) gives \(3g=g\), so \(g=0\) and
\[
 U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p=-z\times Uz.
\]
When \(U\) is invertible, differentiating this identity and using
\[
 U^{\mathsf T}[z]_\times+[z]_\times U
   =(\operatorname{tr}U)[z]_\times-[Uz]_\times
\]
gives
\[
 B=-L[z]_\times U^{-1},\qquad
 L=(\operatorname{tr}U)I-2U^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The constant left kernel is \(\ker L^{\mathsf T}\):
\(B^{\mathsf T}\nu=0\) for every \(z\) is equivalent to
\([z]_\times L^{\mathsf T}\nu=0\) for every \(z\).
Consequently \(L\) is invertible and
\[
 J=\frac{\det L}{\det U}(Uz)(L^{-\mathsf T}z)^{\mathsf T}.
\]

Set \(K=CL^{-\mathsf T}\). From \(JC^{\mathsf T}z=0\) and
\(\mathfrak r=0\), respectively, we obtain
\[
 K+K^{\mathsf T}=0,\qquad
 K^{\mathsf T}U+U^{\mathsf T}K=0.
\]
The second identity, together with the first, says that \(KU\)
is skew-symmetric. Therefore
\[
 C=KL^{\mathsf T}=(\operatorname{tr}U)K-2KU
\]
is skew-symmetric, proving \(A=0\).
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{auto-sing:rank-two-U}
On an open set with \(\Delta=0\), \(\mathscr K=0\), and a
smooth rank-two generator \(U\) of the linear right syzygies, every
point has a neighborhood with a smooth complex frame in which
\[
 \mathbf p(z)=\bigl(h(z),z_0z_2,-z_0z_1\bigr)^{\mathsf T},
\]
where \(h\) is an arbitrary smooth-coefficient quadratic.
In that frame \(u=e_0\), \(\xi=e^0\) satisfy the identity on the neighborhood
\[
 P(u,x)=-\frac12u\odot x+\xi(x)u^2,\qquad \xi(u)=1.
\]
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Choose \(0\ne k\in\ker U\) at a point. The identity
\(U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf p=-z\times Uz\), established above without an
invertibility assumption, implies \(k^{\mathsf T}(z\times Uz)=0\).
Equivalently \([k]_\times U\) is skew-symmetric.
Its left kernel contains \(k\); a three-dimensional skew matrix
with this kernel is a scalar multiple of \([k]_\times\).
Hence
\[
 [k]_\times U=\lambda[k]_\times,\qquad
 U=\lambda I+kt^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The scalar \(\lambda\) cannot be zero, because otherwise
\(\operatorname{rank}U\le1\). From \(Uk=0\) we obtain
\(t^{\mathsf T}k=-\lambda\). Thus
\[
 U^2=\lambda U,\qquad \operatorname{tr}U=2\lambda.
\]
The smooth function \(\lambda=\operatorname{tr}U/2\) is nowhere
zero, so \(U/\lambda\) is a smooth rank-two projector.
Its image and kernel are smooth complementary subbundles. After
shrinking around the chosen point, take local frames of these
subbundles to obtain \(U/\lambda=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1)\).
Scaling the syzygy does not alter \(B(z)Uz=0\).

Under $g\in GL(3,\mathbb C)$,
\[
 B'(z)=(\det g)^{-1}gB(g^{\mathsf T}z)g^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Its linear right syzygy consequently transforms by similarity,
\(U'=g^{-\mathsf T}Ug^{\mathsf T}\), up to its irrelevant scalar.
Thus the projector normalization is an allowed smooth complex frame change.

In this frame,
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}0\\\mathbf p_1\\\mathbf p_2\end{pmatrix}
 =-z\times(0,z_1,z_2)^{\mathsf T}
 =\begin{pmatrix}0\\z_0z_2\\-z_0z_1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first row \(\mathbf p_0=h\) remains arbitrary. The epsilon conversion
now gives
\[
 P(e_0,e_1)=-\frac12e_0\odot e_1,\qquad
 P(e_0,e_2)=-\frac12e_0\odot e_2.
\]
Alternation gives \(P(e_0,e_0)=0\), completing the cut identity.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Let \(O=\{A\ne0\}\). Theorem~\ref{fin14:regular} rules out a
nonempty open set with \(A\ne0\), \(\Delta\not\equiv0\).
If any coefficient of \(\Delta\) were nonzero at a point of \(O\),
it would remain nonzero nearby, giving such a forbidden open set.
Therefore \(\Delta=0\) as a polynomial identity throughout \(O\).

Suppose \(O_0=O\cap\{\mathscr K=0\}\) were nonempty.
This set is open, since absence of a kernel is injectivity of a
finite coefficient map. Choose a point of \(O_0\) and shrink to
a nonempty neighborhood \(U_0\subset O_0\) on which
Lemma~\ref{auto-sing:linear-syzygy} supplies a smooth nowhere-zero
linear syzygy generator \(U\), of rank at least two.
Lemma~\ref{auto-sing:adjugate-equations} gives
\(\mathfrak r=0\) and \(JC^{\mathsf T}z=0\) on \(U_0\).
An invertible value of \(U\) would give \(A=0\) by
Lemma~\ref{auto-sing:invertible-U}; hence \(U\) has rank two
throughout \(U_0\). After a further restriction,
Lemma~\ref{auto-sing:rank-two-U} gives the moving cut on
this nonempty neighborhood, contradicting
Corollary~\ref{r17:no-rank-one-cut}. Thus \(O_0\) is empty.\qedhere
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{hd-scope}\label{thm:nonzero-kernel-all-n}\label{thm:no-common-kernel-open}\label{hd-rank-exclusion}
If $(X,h)$ is compact and connected of complex dimension $n\ge2$,
with constant Chern HSC $c\ne0$,
then $\mathscr K=0$ on an open dense subset of $X$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{hd-transport-lemma}
\begin{equation}\label{hd-B-transport}
 (\nabla_u\mathscr B)(v,w)
 =w(u)\vartheta_v+w\wedge\iota_u\vartheta_v
 -\tfrac12\{T_u\cdot\mathscr B(v,w)
                  +(\iota_u\mathscr B(v,w))\circ T\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:general-curvature-transport} gives the derivative of $P$. Substituting
$2P(\cdot,\cdot)(v,w)=\mathscr B(v,w)+v\wedge w$ gives the transport formula;
the slot contractions and torsion terms are recorded in
Appendix~\ref{app:kernel-transport-calculation}.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{hd-kernel-lemma}
On an open set where $\mathscr K\ne0$,
\begin{equation}\label{hd-kernel-consequences}
 \mathscr K\circ T=0,\qquad \nabla^{1,0}\mathscr K\subset\mathscr K.
\end{equation}
Its Hermitian dual $L$ is holomorphic, and $\nabla^{1,0}E\subset E$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
The coefficient map $v\mapsto\mathscr B(v,\cdot)$ has constant rank
$n-1$, so $\mathscr K$ is a smooth line. For a nonzero section $\nu$,
put $z_u=\nabla_u\nu$ and $\vartheta=\nu\circ T$. Differentiating
$\mathscr B(\nu,w)=0$ and using \eqref{hd-B-transport} gives
\begin{equation}\label{hd-differentiated-kernel}
 \mathscr B(z_u,w)+w(u)\vartheta+w\wedge\iota_u\vartheta=0.
\end{equation}
Set $w=\nu$. Since $\mathscr B(z_u,\nu)=2\nu\wedge z_u$,
wedging with $\nu$ gives $\nu\wedge\vartheta=0$. Choose $u_0$ with
$\nu(u_0)=1$ and contract this identity: $\vartheta=\nu\wedge\alpha$,
where $\alpha=\iota_{u_0}\vartheta$. The same equation now gives
$z_u=-\nu(u)\alpha+\lambda(u)\nu$.
For $u\in\ker\nu$, take $w=\alpha$ in
\eqref{hd-differentiated-kernel}; it gives
$2\alpha(u)\nu\wedge\alpha=0$. Thus $\alpha$ is proportional to
$\nu$, so $\vartheta=0$. The differentiated identity then says
$z_u\in\mathscr K$. Differentiating $\nu(Z)=0$ for $Z\in E$ gives
$\nabla^{1,0}E\subset E$. Metric compatibility then gives
$\nabla^{0,1}L\subset L$, which is holomorphicity.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{hd-global-kernel}
If $X$ is connected and $\mathscr K\ne0$ on an open set, then
$\mathscr K$ is a global real analytic line satisfying
\eqref{hd-kernel-consequences}. Its dual $L$ is holomorphic,
$\nabla^{1,0}E\subset E$, and
\begin{equation}\label{hd-torsion-output}
 T(V,V)\subset E.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
The map $v\mapsto\mathscr B(v,\cdot)$ is real analytic by
Proposition~\ref{univ:analyticity}. Its $n$th exterior power vanishes on
an open set and hence throughout connected $X$. Its rank is at most
$n-1$, and \eqref{hd-kernel-dimension} forces equality everywhere.
Its kernel is therefore an analytic line, and
Lemma~\ref{hd-kernel-lemma} applies globally. The torsion assertion is
$\mathscr K\circ T=0$; the holomorphic line $L$ is integrable.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{hd-defect-equations}
The common-kernel condition implies
\begin{equation}\label{hd-defect-system}
 \begin{aligned}
 D_-{\mathsf S_L}&={\mathsf H_L}-2cI,& D_-{\mathsf B_L}&=-\tfrac12{\mathsf H_L}-aa^*,\\
 {\mathsf H_L}&={\mathsf B_L}^*{\mathsf S_L}={\mathsf S_L}^*{\mathsf B_L},& D_-a&=0,\qquad {\mathsf S_L}^*a=0.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Apply the first Chern Bianchi identity and metric compatibility
to \eqref{hd-kernel-curvature}, using frames adapted to $L\oplus E$.
The off-diagonal connection coefficients contribute $aa^*$, including
in an adapted frame whose induced connection forms vanish at the point.
Appendix~\ref{app:kernel-defect-calculation} computes the curvature
blocks for an arbitrary geodesy defect $a$ and differentiates
$\nu\circ T=0$ to obtain ${\mathsf S_L}^*a=0$.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:nilpotent-defect}
The equations \eqref{hd-defect-system}, with $c\ne0$, imply $a=0$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Work on an open set where $a\ne0$. Set $m=\operatorname{rank} E$, let $C_0$ be
the line spanned by $a$, and let $\pi:E\to E/C_0$ be the quotient.
Then $C_0\subset\ker {\mathsf S_L}^*$, $D_-C_0\subset C_0$, and
$\operatorname{im}(aa^*)\subset C_0$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nilpotent-G}
 \mathcal G=\{v:{\mathsf S_L}^mv=0,\quad\pi {\mathsf B_L}{\mathsf S_L}^jv=0\ (0\le j<m)\}.
\end{equation}
For $v\in\ker {\mathsf S_L}$, ${\mathsf S_L}^*{\mathsf B_L}v={\mathsf B_L}^*{\mathsf S_L}v=0$, so ${\mathsf B_L}$ maps $\ker {\mathsf S_L}$ to
$\ker {\mathsf S_L}^*$. These spaces have equal dimension, whereas quotienting
$\ker {\mathsf S_L}^*$ by $C_0$ lowers its dimension. Thus
$\ker(\pi {\mathsf B_L}|_{\ker {\mathsf S_L}})\ne0$, and $\mathcal G\ne0$.
Restrict to an open set where the defining coefficient map has maximal
rank; $\mathcal G$ is then a positive-rank smooth subbundle. Its definition gives
${\mathsf S_L}\mathcal G\subset \mathcal G$, ${\mathsf B_L}\mathcal G\subset C_0$, and ${\mathsf H_L}\mathcal G={\mathsf S_L}^*{\mathsf B_L}\mathcal G=0$. Hence, for $v\in \mathcal G$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nilpotent-power-derivative}
 (D_-{\mathsf S_L}^j)v
 =\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}{\mathsf S_L}^k({\mathsf H_L}-2cI){\mathsf S_L}^{j-1-k}v
 =-2cj{\mathsf S_L}^{j-1}v.
\end{equation}
The increasing sequence $\ker {\mathsf S_L}^j$ stabilizes by $j=m$, so
$\ker {\mathsf S_L}^{m+1}=\ker {\mathsf S_L}^m$. Differentiating ${\mathsf S_L}^{m+1}v=0$ and using
${\mathsf S_L}^mv=0$ therefore gives ${\mathsf S_L}^mD_-v=0$.
Differentiating $\pi {\mathsf B_L}{\mathsf S_L}^jv=0$ with the quotient connection gives
$\pi {\mathsf B_L}{\mathsf S_L}^jD_-v=0$: the term with $D_-{\mathsf B_L}$ vanishes because
${\mathsf H_L}\mathcal G=0$ and $\operatorname{im}(aa^*)\subset C_0$; the term with $D_-{\mathsf S_L}^j$ vanishes
by \eqref{eq:nilpotent-power-derivative}. Thus $D_-\mathcal G\subset \mathcal G$.
The restriction ${\mathsf S_L}|_\mathcal G$ is nilpotent and has trace zero, but its induced
connection gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nilpotent-trace-contradiction}
 0=D_-\operatorname{tr}({\mathsf S_L}|_\mathcal G)=\operatorname{tr}(({\mathsf H_L}-2cI)|_\mathcal G)=-2c\operatorname{rank} \mathcal G,
\end{equation}
a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:automatic-geodesy}
On any open set where $\mathscr K\ne0$, its Hermitian dual $L$ is
holomorphic and its leaves are Chern totally geodesic.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{hd-kernel-lemma} gives the holomorphic line and the
torsion-output condition. Proposition~\ref{hd-defect-equations} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:nilpotent-defect} give $a=0$.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:common-kernel-structure}
A \emph{totally geodesic common-kernel line} is a holomorphic line
subbundle $L\subset V$ whose leaves are Chern totally geodesic, such that
$E=L^\perp$ is preserved by $\nabla^{1,0}$, $T(V,V)\subset E$, and
every unit section $Y$ of $L$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{neg-common-kernel-curvature}
 R(U,\bar Y,V_0,\bar Z)+R(U,\bar Z,V_0,\bar Y)
 =2c\,\langle U,Y\rangle_h\langle V_0,Z\rangle_h.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lemma:normal-degree-all-n}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:global-normal-curvature}\label{eq:global-degree-form}
 \nabla_{\bar t}{\mathsf S_L}_t=2c\,h_{t\bar t}I_N-2R^N_{t\bar t},\qquad i\operatorname{tr} R^N=(n-1)c\,\omega_h|_\Sigma+\frac i2\bar\partial\beta.
\end{equation}
For a compact leaf,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:global-degree}
 \deg N=\frac{(n-1)c}{2\pi}\operatorname{Area}_h(\Sigma).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
In a unit tangent frame, first Bianchi and \eqref{hd-curvature-H} give
$D_{\bar Y}{\mathsf S_L}_Y=2cI_N-2\pi_ER(Y,\bar Y)|_E$.
The last operator is the curvature of the quotient connection along the
leaf, proving the first identity. Taking the trace
gives the second, since
$\bar\partial\beta=-\partial_{\bar t}\operatorname{tr}({\mathsf S_L}_t)\,dt\wedge d\bar t$.
On a curve $\bar\partial\beta=d\beta$; integration gives the degree.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:positive-kernel-all-n}
A compact Hermitian manifold with constant Chern HSC $c>0$ admits
no line satisfying Definition~\ref{def:common-kernel-structure}.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Since the leaves are real totally geodesic, the ambient geodesic
spray is tangent to their unit tangent bundle. This bundle is compact:
it is the unit circle bundle of the global real plane distribution
underlying $L$ over compact $X$. The restricted spray is therefore
complete. Its projected curves are the intrinsic geodesics of the
leaves, so every leaf is complete in its intrinsic metric.

Each leaf is therefore a complete surface with Gaussian curvature
$c>0$. Bonnet--Myers gives diameter at most $\pi/\sqrt c$, and
Hopf--Rinow makes it compact. These are intrinsic statements about the
complete leaf; they do not require it to be embedded.

The normal bundle has a flat complex Bott connection: In a holomorphic foliation chart $(t,z^1,\ldots,z^{n-1})$
with plaques given by constant $z$, declare the normal classes
$[\partial/\partial z^\alpha]$ parallel along each plaque.
On an overlap, the transverse coordinates have the form $z'=F(z)$,
so the normal transition matrix is constant along each plaque.
These local connections therefore glue to a flat complex connection
on $N|_\Sigma$. Its determinant connection is flat, and hence
$\deg N=0$ by Chern--Weil theory. This contradicts
\eqref{eq:global-degree}, since $n\ge2$, $c>0$, and the leaf has
positive area.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{neg-differential-system}
\begin{gather}
 {\mathsf H_L}={\mathsf H_L}^*,\qquad D_-{\mathsf S_L}={\mathsf H_L}-2cI,\qquad D_-{\mathsf B_L}=-\tfrac12{\mathsf H_L},
 \label{neg-mixed-system}\\
 D_+{\mathsf B_L}=-{\mathsf B_L}({\mathsf B_L}+{\mathsf S_L}),\label{neg-pure-Riccati}\\
 D_-{\mathsf H_L}=-{\mathsf S_L}^*{\mathsf H_L}-2c{\mathsf B_L}^*,\qquad D_+{\mathsf H_L}=-{\mathsf H_L}{\mathsf S_L}-2c{\mathsf B_L}.
 \label{neg-H-derivatives}
\end{gather}
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
The mixed equations are \eqref{hd-defect-system} with $a=0$.
The $(2,0)$ curvature identity $R(X_0,Y)Y=0$ gives the equation for
$D_+{\mathsf B_L}$, and differentiating ${\mathsf H_L}={\mathsf B_L}^*{\mathsf S_L}$ gives the two derivatives of ${\mathsf H_L}$.
The connection and curvature calculations are in
Appendix~\ref{app:kernel-differential-calculation}.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{neg-divergence-lemma}
For a real function $\psi$,
\begin{align}
 \operatorname{div}Z_w
 &=\operatorname{Re}(D_-w)+\operatorname{Re}(\overline w(\beta+s)),\label{neg-divergence}\\
 \operatorname{div}(\psi{}Z_w)
 &=\psi\operatorname{Re}(D_-w)+\operatorname{Re}(\overline w\{\psi(\beta+s)+Y\psi\}).
 \label{neg-weighted-divergence}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
The connection trace splits into its horizontal and leaf parts;
the torsion trace contributes the remaining $s$ term. This gives
the first identity, and the product rule gives the second.
Appendix~\ref{app:kernel-divergence-calculation} records the coordinate
calculation with the connection on every tensor slot retained.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{neg-kernel-reduction}
On an open set where $\operatorname{rank} {\mathsf B_L}=r\ge1$, $\ker {\mathsf B_L}=\ker {\mathsf B_L}^*$.
For $W=(\ker {\mathsf B_L})^\perp$ and its orthogonal projection $\Pi$,
\begin{equation}\label{neg-active-block}
 {\mathsf B_L}=\Pi {\mathsf B_L}\Pi,\qquad {\mathsf H_L}=\Pi {\mathsf H_L}\Pi,\qquad
 {\mathsf B_L}_W:={\mathsf B_L}|_W\text{ is invertible},\qquad D_\pm\Pi=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
For $v\in\ker {\mathsf B_L}$, ${\mathsf H_L}v={\mathsf S_L}^*{\mathsf B_L}v=0$. Differentiating ${\mathsf B_L}v=0$ and using
$D_-{\mathsf B_L}=-{\mathsf S_L}^*{\mathsf B_L}/2$ gives $D_-v\in\ker {\mathsf B_L}$. Differentiating ${\mathsf H_L}v=0$
then gives $0=(D_-{\mathsf H_L})v=-2c{\mathsf B_L}^*v$. Thus $\ker {\mathsf B_L}\subset\ker {\mathsf B_L}^*$;
equality of dimensions gives equality of kernels, and hence the block
statements. Differentiating $\Pi {\mathsf B_L}={\mathsf B_L}={\mathsf B_L}\Pi$ yields
$(D_-\Pi){\mathsf B_L}={\mathsf B_L}(D_-\Pi)=0$. The derivative of $\Pi^2=\Pi$ has only
off-diagonal blocks, both killed by the invertible ${\mathsf B_L}_W$.
Thus $D_-\Pi=0$, and taking adjoints gives $D_+\Pi=0$.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:neg-kernel-exclusion}
A compact Hermitian manifold with constant Chern HSC $c<0$ admits
no line satisfying Definition~\ref{def:common-kernel-structure}.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
Suppose first that ${\mathsf B_L}$ is nonzero somewhere. Put $r=\max_X\operatorname{rank} {\mathsf B_L}\ge1$
and $\mathcal U_r=\{\operatorname{rank} {\mathsf B_L}=r\}$. The global characteristic coefficient
\begin{equation}\label{neg-characteristic-coefficient}
 e_r({\mathsf B_L})=\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^r{\mathsf B_L})\in\Gamma((L^*)^{\otimes r})
\end{equation}
satisfies, by Lemma~\ref{neg-kernel-reduction},
\begin{equation}\label{neg-maximal-rank-locus}
 e_r({\mathsf B_L})=\det {\mathsf B_L}_W\ne0\text{ on }\mathcal U_r,\qquad
 \mathcal U_r=\{|e_r({\mathsf B_L})|>0\}.
\end{equation}
On this set put $a_1=\operatorname{tr}(\Pi {\mathsf S_L})$, $a_0=\operatorname{tr}((I-\Pi){\mathsf S_L})$,
and the real function $t_{\mathsf H_L}=\operatorname{tr} {\mathsf H_L}$, so $s=a_1+a_0$.
The sections $a_1,a_0$ of $L^*$ obey
\begin{equation}\label{neg-projection-bounds}
 |a_1|\le\sqrt r\,|{\mathsf S_L}|,\qquad |a_0|\le\sqrt{m-r}\,|{\mathsf S_L}|.
\end{equation}
Taking traces in \eqref{neg-mixed-system} gives
\begin{equation}\label{neg-trace-equations}
 D_-\beta=-t_{\mathsf H_L}/2,\qquad D_-a_1=t_{\mathsf H_L}-2cr,\qquad
 D_-a_0=-2c(m-r).
\end{equation}
Since $D_\pm\Pi=0$, compression to $W$ gives
$D_+{\mathsf B_L}_W=-{\mathsf B_L}_W({\mathsf B_L}_W+{\mathsf S_L}_W)$ and $D_-{\mathsf B_L}_W=-{\mathsf S_L}_W^*{\mathsf B_L}_W/2$,
where ${\mathsf S_L}_W=\Pi {\mathsf S_L}|_W$. Jacobi's determinant formula therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{neg-characteristic-derivatives}
 D_+e_r=-(\beta+a_1)e_r,\qquad
 D_-e_r=-\tfrac12\overline{a_1}e_r.
\end{equation}
For the smooth global function $\gamma=|e_r({\mathsf B_L})|^2$, this implies
\begin{equation}\label{neg-characteristic-norm}
 Y\gamma=-(\beta+\tfrac32a_1)\gamma.
\end{equation}
The weight is forced by the term $t_{\mathsf H_L}$, which has no sign.
For a tentative weight $\psi_\sigma=\gamma^\sigma$, set
\[
v_\sigma=\psi_\sigma^{-1}\{
\psi_\sigma(\beta+s)+Y\psi_\sigma\}
=(1-\sigma)\beta+(1-3\sigma/2)a_1+a_0.
\]
Using \eqref{neg-trace-equations} gives
\[
D_-v_\sigma=(\tfrac12-\sigma)t_{\mathsf H_L}-2c(m-3\sigma r/2).
\]
Thus $\sigma=1/2$ is the unique power that removes $t_{\mathsf H_L}$.
Choose $\psi=\sqrt\gamma$ and multiply $v_{1/2}$ by four:
$w_r=2\beta+a_1+4a_0$. Then
\[
D_-w_r=-2c(4m-3r),\qquad
\psi(\beta+s)+Y\psi=\tfrac14\psi{}w_r.
\]
Equation~\eqref{neg-weighted-divergence} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{neg-maximal-rank-divergence}
 \operatorname{div}(\psi{}Z_{w_r})
 =\psi\left[-2c(4m-3r)+\tfrac14|w_r|^2\right]
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal U_r.
\end{equation}
The bracket is positive, since $c<0$ and $4m-3r\ge m>0$.

To integrate across the rank-drop set, choose a smooth cutoff
$\chi:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$, zero on $[0,1]$ and one on $[4,\infty)$.
Extend $V_\varepsilon=\chi(\gamma/\varepsilon^2)\sqrt\gamma\,Z_{w_r}$
by zero outside $\mathcal U_r$; it is smooth on $X$.
Compactness and \eqref{neg-projection-bounds}--\eqref{neg-characteristic-norm}
give $|Z_{w_r}\gamma|\le C\gamma$. On the cutoff annulus
$\varepsilon\le\sqrt\gamma\le2\varepsilon$,
\begin{equation}\label{neg-cutoff-error}
 \left|\sqrt\gamma\,
 \frac{\chi'(\gamma/\varepsilon^2)}{\varepsilon^2}
 Z_{w_r}\gamma\right|\le C\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Integrate $\operatorname{div}V_\varepsilon$ and let
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The error tends to zero, and dominated
convergence gives
\begin{equation}\label{neg-maximal-rank-integral}
 0=\int_{\mathcal U_r}|e_r({\mathsf B_L})|
 \left[-2c(4m-3r)+\tfrac14|w_r|^2\right]\,dV_h,
\end{equation}
contradicting positivity on the nonempty open set $\mathcal U_r$.
Thus ${\mathsf B_L}=0$, so $\beta={\mathsf H_L}=0$ and $D_-s=-2cm$.
Finally \eqref{neg-divergence} gives
\[
 0=\int_X\operatorname{div}Z_s\,dV_h
  =\int_X(-2cm+|s|^2)\,dV_h>0,
\]
a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
A kernel on an open set extends globally by
Proposition~\ref{hd-global-kernel}. Theorem~\ref{thm:automatic-geodesy}
makes its dual a totally geodesic common-kernel line, contradicting
Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-kernel-all-n} or
Theorem~\ref{thm:neg-kernel-exclusion}, according to the sign of $c$.
The zero-kernel locus is open because the defining bundle map has full
rank there; its complement has empty interior by the preceding argument.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
If $A$ were nonzero at a point, it would remain nonzero on a
nonempty open set.  Then Theorem~\ref{auto-sing:local-alternative} would
contradict Theorem~\ref{thm:no-common-kernel-open}.  Thus $A=0$ everywhere.

Equation~\eqref{b:eq:primitive} now gives
$d\omega_h=\theta\wedge\omega_h$, where
$\theta=-(\eta+\bar\eta)/2$.  Applying $d$ yields
$d\theta\wedge\omega_h=0$.  Wedge multiplication by $\omega_h$
is injective on two-forms in real dimension six: with adjoint
$\Lambda$, the pointwise Lefschetz identity gives
\[
 \|\omega_h\wedge\alpha\|^2
 =\|\alpha\|^2+\|\Lambda\alpha\|^2.
\]
Therefore $d\theta=0$, and $h$ is locally conformally K\"ahler.
Huang--Wan's constant Chern holomorphic sectional curvature theorem
\cite[Theorem~1.2, p.~3]{HW26} makes the given metric K\"ahler.

Compactness gives completeness, which passes to the lifted metric
on the universal cover. The complete simply connected K\"ahler
classification \cite[Chapter~IX, \S7, Theorems~7.8--7.9,
\mbox{pp.}~169--171]{KN69} identifies that cover with scaled $\mathbb P^3$
for $c>0$ and complex hyperbolic three-space for $c<0$.
The deck group acts freely and properly discontinuously by
holomorphic isometries, and the quotient is compact.
In the positive case every projective unitary transformation has
an eigenline and therefore a fixed point. Thus the deck group is
trivial. In the negative case it gives the asserted compact
complex-hyperbolic quotient.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:bianchi1}\label{c0:r1:bianchi}
If $H_h\equiv0$, the common identity \eqref{eq:fund-barC} gives
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:E}\label{c0:r1:etabar}
 B_\eta=2(\Xi^{\mathsf T}+\beta^Q),\qquad \operatorname{tr}\Xi=0.
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:scal}
 s=2\operatorname{tr} Q=-\hat s,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr} B_\eta=\textstyle\sum_p\nabla_{\bar p}\eta_p=2s.
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:barA}\label{c0:r1:Sbar}
\begin{aligned}
 \nabla_{\bar j}A^{al}
 &=-(\mathcal P^{a,jl}+\mathcal P^{l,ja})-(\varepsilon_{jlb}Q_{ab}+\varepsilon_{jab}Q_{lb}),\\
 S&:=\operatorname{Sym}(\nabla''A)=-2\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal P .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The first Chern--Ricci tensor also satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{c0:r1:ricci-lee}
 \rho_{i\bar j}^{(1)}-\tfrac12\nabla_{\bar j}\eta_i
 =\overline{\Xi_{ij}},\qquad \operatorname{tr}_h\rho^{(1)}=2\tau.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
Contract \eqref{eq:fund-barC} with $\varepsilon_{pal}$ and use
$\eta_p=\sum_{a,k}\varepsilon_{pak}C^{ak}$ to obtain \eqref{c0:eq:E}.
The trace of $\Xi$ is zero by symmetry of the last two slots of $\mathcal P$.
Tracing \eqref{c0:eq:decomp} gives \eqref{c0:eq:scal} and
$\rho^{(1)}=\Xi^{\mathsf T}+\overline\Xi+\beta^Q$, which proves
\eqref{c0:r1:ricci-lee}. Finally, the symmetric part in $(a,l)$ of
\eqref{eq:fund-barC} is \eqref{c0:eq:barA}; its $Q$ terms vanish
under total symmetrization.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:J1}
For $W$ as defined in \eqref{c0:r1:definitions}, on every Hermitian threefold,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:J1}
 (\partial\eta)_{qp}=\sum_r\varepsilon_{qpr}\nu^r,\qquad \nu^l=2\sum_aW_a^{al}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
Since $R$ has no $(2,0)$-part, the $(3,0)$-component of the first Bianchi identity of a connection with torsion reads $\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}(i,j,k)}\bigl(\nabla_iT^l_{jk}+T^m_{ij}T^l_{mk}\bigr)=0$; take $(i,j,k)=(0,1,2)$. With $T^l_{jk}=\varepsilon_{jka}C^{al}$ the derivative terms are $\sum_a\nabla_aC^{al}$, and the quadratic terms are $\sum_{k,m,b}C^{km}\varepsilon_{mkb}C^{bl}=-\sum_b\eta_bC^{bl}=-(\eta A)^l$. Next, $\sum_a\nabla_aA^{al}=\frac12(\eta A)^l+\sum_aW_a^{al}$, and $\sum_{a,m}\varepsilon_{alm}\nabla_a\eta_m=\frac12\sum_{a,m}\varepsilon_{alm}a_{am}$. Define $\nu$ by $(\partial\eta)_{am}=\sum_s\varepsilon_{ams}\nu^s$. By \eqref{c0:eq:a}, $a_{am}=\varepsilon_{ams}\nu^s-\varepsilon_{amb}C^{br}\eta_r$, and $\sum_{a,m}\varepsilon_{alm}\varepsilon_{ams}=-2\delta_{ls}$, $\sum_{a,m}\varepsilon_{alm}\varepsilon_{amb}C^{br}\eta_r=-2(A\eta)^l$. Hence $\sum_a\nabla_aC^{al}=(\eta A)^l+\sum_aW_a^{al}-\frac12\nu^l$, and the Bianchi identity gives $\nu^l=2\sum_aW_a^{al}$.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:transalg}
Let $V^a$ be a vector and $N_{pa}$ a matrix. The system
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:transsys}
 \varepsilon_{ika}N_{pa}-\varepsilon_{pka}N_{ia}=T^r_{ip}\varepsilon_{rka}V^a\qquad(\text{all }p,i,k)
\end{equation}
has the unique solution $N_{pc}=(M_pV)^c$.
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
Contract with $\varepsilon_{ikc}$. The left side becomes $N_{pc}+\delta_{pc}\operatorname{tr} N$. Using $T^r_{ip}=\varepsilon_{ipd}C^{dr}$ and $\sum_{k,r}C^{kr}\varepsilon_{rka}=-\eta_a$, the right side becomes $\sum_{r,a}C^{cr}\varepsilon_{rpa}V^a+\delta_{pc}\eta_aV^a$. Taking the trace gives $\operatorname{tr} N=\frac12\eta_aV^a$, and inserting $C$ yields $N_{pc}=\sum_{r,a}A^{cr}\varepsilon_{rpa}V^a+\frac12\eta_pV^c$. The map $N\mapsto$ left side is injective, so the contraction loses nothing.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:Ptransport}
If $H_h\equiv0$, the $(j,l)$-symmetric part of \eqref{c0:eq:bianchi2} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:Ptransport}\label{c0:r1:Utransport}\label{c0:transport}
 \nabla_p\mathcal P^{a,jl}=\sum_e(M_p)_{ae}\mathcal P^{e,jl}
 =\sum_eT^\circ{}^a_{pe}\mathcal P^{e,jl}+\tfrac12\eta_p\mathcal P^{a,jl}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
The transport identity is \cite[Lemma~3, equation~(2.15)]{ChenZhengThreefold2026}.
The asserted equivalence is the algebraic identification
\eqref{c0:eq:transsys}, with $V^a=\mathcal P^{a,jl}$ and
$N_{pa}=\nabla_p\mathcal P^{a,jl}$, for each symmetric pair $(j,l)$.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:Qtr}
Put $Y_m:=\nabla_{\bar m}\mathcal P$ and define the component contraction
$\mathfrak c_b:=\sum_{k,r}A^{kr}\overline{\mathcal P^{b,rk}}$.
If $H_h\equiv0$,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:Qtr}
 \nabla_kQ_{cb}=\tfrac12\eta_kQ_{cb}+(A\mathsf J_kQ)_{cb}+\sum_rC^{cr}\,\overline{\mathcal P^{b,rk}}-\tfrac12\delta_{ck}\mathfrak c_b-\sum_{i,m}\varepsilon_{imc}\,\overline{Y_m^{b,ik}},
\end{equation}
and $\nabla_{\bar k}Q_{cb}=\overline{\nabla_kQ_{bc}}$.
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
The $(j,l)$-alternating part of $R$ is $\varepsilon_{jlb}V_b(i,k)$ with $V_b(i,k)=\overline{\mathcal P^{b,ik}}+\varepsilon_{ika}Q_{ab}$, and \eqref{c0:eq:bianchi2} gives $\nabla_pV_b(i,k)-\nabla_iV_b(p,k)=T^r_{ip}V_b(r,k)$. Contract with $\varepsilon_{ipc}$. The $\mathcal P$-terms give $2\sum_{i,p}\varepsilon_{ipc}\nabla_p\overline{\mathcal P^{b,ik}}$, the $Q$-terms give $2\nabla_kQ_{cb}-2\delta_{ck}(\operatorname{div}Q)_b$ with $(\operatorname{div}Q)_b=\sum_a\nabla_aQ_{ab}$, and the right side gives $2\sum_rC^{cr}V_b(r,k)$. The trace $c=k$ yields $(\operatorname{div}Q)_b=-\frac12\mathfrak c_b+\frac12(\eta Q)_b$ (the $\mathcal P$-term drops by symmetry, and $\sum_{k,r}C^{kr}\varepsilon_{rka}=-\eta_a$). Substituting back and inserting $C=A+\frac12\varepsilon\eta$ gives \eqref{c0:eq:Qtr}, since $\nabla_p\overline{\mathcal P}=\overline{\nabla_{\bar p}\mathcal P}$. The last statement is $Q=Q^*$.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- lemma-38: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:MA}
Put $\widehat Q_p:=\nabla_pQ-\frac12\eta_pQ$ and $T^\circ{}_p:=A\mathsf J_p$. If $H_h\equiv0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:MA}
 \nabla_{\bar l}W_p^{aj}=-(T^\circ{}_p\mathcal P)^{a,lj}-(T^\circ{}_p\mathcal P)^{j,la}-\varepsilon_{ljb}(\widehat Q_p)_{ab}-\varepsilon_{lab}(\widehat Q_p)_{jb}-(R_{p\bar l}\cdot A)^{aj}-\tfrac12(B_\eta)_{p\bar l}A^{aj},
\end{equation}
where $(R_{p\bar l}\cdot A)^{aj}=\sum_mR_{p\bar lm\bar a}A^{mj}+\sum_mR_{p\bar lm\bar j}A^{am}-\rho_{p\bar l}A^{aj}$ includes the $K_X$-factor.
<!-- end lemma-38 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
By \eqref{c0:eq:ricci}, $\nabla_{\bar l}\nabla_pA=\nabla_p\nabla_{\bar l}A-R_{p\bar l}\cdot A$. The left side equals $\frac12(B_\eta)_{p\bar l}A+\frac12\eta_p\nabla_{\bar l}A+\nabla_{\bar l}W_p$. Differentiate \eqref{c0:eq:barA} with \eqref{c0:eq:Ptransport}: $\nabla_p\nabla_{\bar l}A^{aj}=-(M_p\mathcal P)^{a,lj}-(M_p\mathcal P)^{j,la}-\varepsilon_{ljb}\nabla_pQ_{ab}-\varepsilon_{lab}\nabla_pQ_{jb}$. The $\frac12\eta_p$-parts of $M_p\mathcal P$ and of $\nabla_pQ$ combine with $-\frac12\eta_p\nabla_{\bar l}A$ into the stated form.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- lemma-39: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:mixed}
For every metric with $H_h\equiv0$, let $W$ be as in
\eqref{c0:r1:definitions}. With the index $\bar l$ raised by $h$ and
$\rho^{(1)}_{p\bar l}=\sum_kR_{p\bar lk\bar k}$,
\[
 \operatorname{Sym}_{(a,j,l)}\nabla_{\bar l}W_p^{aj}
 =-\operatorname{Sym}_{(a,j,l)}\bigl[(\tfrac12(B_\eta)_{p\bar l}-\rho^{(1)}_{p\bar l})A^{aj}\bigr]
 =\operatorname{Sym}_{(a,j,l)}\bigl[\,\overline{\Xi_{pl}}\,A^{aj}\bigr].
\]
<!-- end lemma-39 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
Apply \cite[Lemma~3, equation~(2.17)]{ChenZhengThreefold2026}
with $\mathcal B=A$, $\mathcal N=W$, and $G^*=-2\overline\Xi$.
Both symmetrizations are averages and both include the canonical factor.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- lemma-40: body_md -->
\label{c0:r1:hessian}\label{c0:up:fullhessian}
For every zero-Chern-HSC threefold,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:r1:p-hessian}\label{c0:up:hessian}
 p_{i\bar j}-\tfrac12\eta_i p_{\bar j}-\tfrac12\bar\eta_jp_i
 +\tfrac14p\eta_i\bar\eta_j
 =p\rho^{(1)}_{i\bar j}-2\mathsf G(W)_{i\bar j}-4\mathsf M(\mathcal P)_{i\bar j}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-40 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
The calculation in Appendix~\ref{c0:app:fullhessian}
differentiates the sourced second Bianchi equation,
retains the freely occurring $\nabla'\bar\mathcal P$, and uses the curvature
action on all three vector slots and the canonical line. No rank or
positivity assumption is used.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- lemma-41: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:div}
For a $(1,0)$-vector field $X$, $d(\iota_XdV)=(\operatorname{div}X)\,dV$ with $\operatorname{div}X=\sum_p\nabla_pX^p-\eta_pX^p$ in unitary frames. Consequently, if $H_h\equiv0$,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:stokes}
 2\int_Xs\,dV_h=\int_X|\eta|^2\,dV_h,\qquad \int_X\operatorname{tr} Q\,dV_h=\tfrac14\int_X|\eta|^2\,dV_h .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-41 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
The vector formula is the coordinate divergence identity underlying
\cite[Lemma~4, equation~(3.6)]{ChenZhengThreefold2026}.
Its integrated consequences follow from equation~(3.3) there,
with unit test function and
$\chi=2s=4\operatorname{tr} Q$, yielding \eqref{c0:eq:stokes}.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- lemma-42: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:F}
For real $u,v\in C^\infty(X)$, with $Lu:=\Delta u-\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,\partial u\rangle_h$,
\[
 \int_XvLu\,dV_h=-\operatorname{Re}\int_X\langle\partial u,\partial v\rangle\,dV_h,\qquad
 \int_Xu\,\mathscr L u\,dV_h=-\int_X\bigl|\partial u-\tfrac12u\eta\bigr|^2\,dV_h .\tag{F}\label{c0:eq:F}
\]
Hence $\mathscr L$ is formally self-adjoint.
<!-- end lemma-42 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->
Apply \cite[Lemma~4, equations~(3.2)--(3.4)]{ChenZhengThreefold2026}
with $P=-\mathscr L$ and unit weight. The cited formulas use the original
Hermitian volume and include its torsion-trace correction.
<!-- end proof-80 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:P}
If $H_h\equiv0$ then, with $S=\operatorname{Sym}(\nabla''A)$ as in \eqref{c0:eq:barA} and ordered norms,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:P}
 \mathscr L \delta_0=\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{def}}:=\bigl|\nabla'T^\circ{}-\tfrac12\eta\otimes T^\circ{}\bigr|^2+3|S|^2\ \ge0 ,\qquad \delta_0=|T^\circ{}|^2-2s=2|A|^2-4\operatorname{tr} Q.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-81: body_md -->
In \cite[Proposition~2, equation~(3.15)]{ChenZhengThreefold2026},
substitute $P=-\mathscr L$, $\psi=-\delta_0$, and $\mathcal N=W$.
The parallel alternating-symbol identification gives
$|\nabla'T^\circ-\eta\otimes T^\circ/2|^2=2|W|^2$,
which is the displayed convention change.
<!-- end proof-81 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:barred}
Put $a_{ik}:=\nabla_i\eta_k-\nabla_k\eta_i$ and, for a $(1,0)$-form index $p$,
\[
 b_p=\textstyle\sum_{l,i,k} T^\circ{}^l_{ik}\overline{\nabla_{\bar p}T^\circ{}^l_{ik}},\quad
 c_p=2\sum_{a,l} A^{al}\overline{S^{alp}},\quad
 r_p=-\sum_{i,k} a_{ik}\overline{T^\circ{}^p_{ik}} .
\]
If $H_h\equiv0$ then pointwise $|\nabla''T^\circ{}|^2+\frac12|a|^2-6|S|^2=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{div}X$ with $X^q=h^{q\bar p}\overline{(b-3c-r)_p}$; hence
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:barred}
 \int_X\Bigl(|\nabla''T^\circ{}|^2+\tfrac12|a|^2\Bigr)\,dV_h=6\int_X|S|^2\,dV_h .
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-82: body_md -->
The pointwise divergence identity, including its free second-derivative
cancellation, is proved in Appendix~\ref{c0:app:barred-proof}. Integrate it
using Lemma~\ref{c0:lem:div}. The left side consists of two squared norms;
therefore $S=0$ forces both $\nabla''T^\circ=0$ and $a=0$.
<!-- end proof-82 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{c0:thm:A}
On a compact connected zero-Chern-HSC threefold, either the original
metric is Chern flat or
\[
 p=4\operatorname{tr}Q-2|A|^2>0
\]
everywhere.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-83: body_md -->
Write $\delta=\delta_0=-p$ and
$D v=\partial v-v\eta/2$ for real functions $v$.
By the negative-part test and path argument in
\cite[Lemma~4, equation~(3.5), and the proof of Proposition~3]{ChenZhengThreefold2026},
$\delta_+=\max\{\delta,0\}$ satisfies
$D\delta_+=0$ almost everywhere and $\int_X\delta_+\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{def}}\,dV=0$.
If $\delta_+\not\equiv0$, that path argument gives
$\delta=\delta_+>0$ everywhere, hence $\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{def}}=0$.
This implication does not require a nonzero-source assumption.
The scalar and barred-energy identities give
\[
 \nabla'T^\circ=\eta\otimes T^\circ/2,
 \qquad \nabla''T^\circ=0.
\]
Put $v=|T^\circ|^2$. Since $Dv=D\delta=0$, the quotient
$v/\delta$ is a constant $C\ge0$. Hence
\[
 \eta=2\partial\log\delta,\qquad
 \Delta\log\delta=s=\tfrac12(C-1)\delta.
\]
The extrema of $\log\delta$ force $s=0$; the maximum principle
then makes $\delta$ constant and $\eta=0$.
Now $T=T^\circ$ and $\nabla''T=0$, so first Bianchi and
zero-HSC polarization give $R=0$.

It remains to consider $\delta\le0$.
If $\delta$ vanishes at a point, choose a constant
$d\ge\max_X\max\{|\eta|^2/4-s,0\}$. Then
\[
 (\mathscr L-d)\delta=\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{def}}-d\delta\ge0.
\]
The zeroth-order coefficient is nonpositive, and $\delta$ has
maximum zero. The strong maximum principle gives $\delta\equiv0$.
Thus again $\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{def}}=0$, $\nabla''T^\circ=0$, and
$\partial v=v\eta/2$, now with $v=2s$.
If $v$ had a positive maximum, then near that point
$\eta=2\partial\log v$ and
$\Delta\log v=s=v/2>0$, a contradiction.
Hence $v=s=0$. Equation~\eqref{c0:eq:stokes} gives $\eta=0$,
and zero-HSC polarization again gives $R=0$.
Consequently every nonflat metric satisfies $\delta<0$, as claimed.
<!-- end proof-83 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:primitive-energy}
On a compact zero-Chern-HSC threefold,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:primitive-energy}
 \int_Xu\,\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(G^2)\,\,dV_h
 \ge 6\int_Xu\bigl(|W|^2+|S|^2\bigr)\,\,dV_h
       +\frac83\int_Xu^3\,\,dV_h+2\int_Xpu^2\,\,dV_h.
\end{equation}
The inequality itself requires no sign assumption on $p$ and no
restriction on the output rank of $\mathcal P$. All norms are ordered-index
norms, with the exterior-metric convention for $\partial\eta$.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-84: body_md -->
Take weight one in \cite[Proposition~1, equations~(3.9)--(3.10)]{ChenZhengThreefold2026}.
With $K=A^*A$, $K_0=K-uI/3$, and $w$ as defined in
Appendix~\ref{c0:app:energy-completion}, use
$|A^*w|^2\le u|w|^2$, $|K_0|^2\le2u^2/3$, and $\chi=p+2u$;
discard the nonnegative squares and multiply by six.
This uses Proposition~1, not the nonzero-source hypothesis in their
Proposition~3. The underlying identities are recorded, without
rederivation, in Appendix~\ref{c0:app:energy-completion}.
<!-- end proof-84 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:rank3}
On an open set where $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal P=3$ (as a map $\operatorname{Sym}^2(T^{*1,0}X)\to T^{1,0}X\otimes K_X$),
\[
 \partial\eta=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla'A=\tfrac12\eta\otimes A .
\]
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-85: body_md -->
Differentiate \eqref{c0:eq:Ptransport} and use the pure commutator formula $\nabla^2_{q,p}-\nabla^2_{p,q}=-T^r_{qp}\nabla_r$ : $\widetilde\Omega_{qp}\mathcal P=0$ with
\[
 \widetilde\Omega_{qp}:=(\nabla_qM)_p-(\nabla_pM)_q+[M_p,M_q]+T^r_{qp}M_r .
\]
If $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal P=3$ then $\widetilde\Omega=0$. Write $\nabla_qA=\frac12\eta_qA+X_q$. Using $T^r_{qp}=T^\circ{}^r_{qp}+\frac12(\eta_p\delta^r_q-\eta_q\delta^r_p)$, all terms containing $\eta\otimes A$ cancel and
\[
 \widetilde\Omega_{qp}=X_q\mathsf J_p-X_p\mathsf J_q
 +\bigl(A\mathsf J_pA\mathsf J_q-A\mathsf J_qA\mathsf J_p+T^\circ{}^r_{qp}A\mathsf J_r\bigr)+\tfrac12(\partial\eta)_{qp}I .
\]
The bracket vanishes identically for symmetric $A$; the expansion
and cancellation hold without a rank assumption and will also be used
below. At full rank, the local compatibility calculation in
\cite[proof of Proposition~4, equations~(4.3)--(4.5)]{ChenZhengThreefold2026}
gives $\partial\eta=0$ and $X=0$.
<!-- end proof-85 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{c0:r2:parallel}
On every constant-output-rank-two open set of a smooth
zero-Chern-HSC Hermitian threefold, $\partial\eta=0$.
Equivalently, $k=B_W\ell=0$ in every local annihilator gauge,
with $B_W$ defined by \eqref{c0:eq:Kform}.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- lemma-43: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:pureprol}
On $\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}$:
\textup{(a)} $q_{\ell}\kappa_{\ell}=0$;
\textup{(b)} if $\kappa_{\ell}\equiv0$ on an open set $V$, then $q_{\ell}\,k=0$ on $V$;
\textup{(c)} if $k\equiv0$ on an open set $V$, then $q_{\ell}\,B_W=0$ on $V$.
<!-- end lemma-43 -->
<!-- proof-86: body_md -->
Work at a point in a unitary frame with $\ell=e^2$ there (rescale $\ell$; the statements are homogeneous). Then $\ell_0=\ell_1=0$, $r^2=q_{\ell}$, $k^2=\kappa_{\ell}$, and from \eqref{c0:eq:elltr}: $\nabla_0\ell_1=-q_{\ell}$, $\nabla_1\ell_0=q_{\ell}$, $\nabla_0\ell_2=\gamma_0-\frac12\eta_0+r^1$, $\nabla_2\ell_0=-r^1$. We use $\nabla_qW_p=(\nabla_q\ell_p)B_W+\ell_pH_q-\frac13(e_p(\nabla_qk)^{\mathsf T}+(\nabla_qk)e_p^{\mathsf T})$ with $\nabla_qk=H_q\ell+B_W\nabla_q\ell$, $T^2_{01}=C^{22}=q_{\ell}$, $(\partial\eta)_{01}=-\frac23\kappa_{\ell}$, $(\partial\eta)_{02}=\frac23k^1$, and $W_r^{22}=\ell_r\kappa_{\ell}-\frac23\delta_{r2}\kappa_{\ell}$.

(a) The $(2,2)$-entry of \eqref{c0:eq:I1} for $(q,p)=(0,1)$: the left side is $(\nabla_0\ell_1-\nabla_1\ell_0)\kappa_{\ell}=-2q_{\ell}\kappa_{\ell}$; the right side is $-T^2_{01}W_2^{22}-\frac12(\partial\eta)_{01}q_{\ell}=-\frac13q_{\ell}\kappa_{\ell}+\frac13q_{\ell}\kappa_{\ell}=0$.

(b) Now $\kappa_{\ell}=0$ and $\nabla\kappa_{\ell}=0$. Since $\nabla_p\kappa_{\ell}=H_p^{22}+2(\gamma_p-\frac12\eta_p)\kappa_{\ell}-2\sum\varepsilon_{pac}k^ar^c$, we get $H_p^{22}=2(k\times r)_p$ with $(k\times r)_p=\sum_{a,c}\varepsilon_{pac}k^ar^c$; in particular $(k\times r)_0=k^1q_{\ell}$. Also $(\nabla_0k)^2=H_0^{22}-(k\times r)_0=k^1q_{\ell}$. The $(2,2)$-entry of \eqref{c0:eq:I1} for $(q,p)=(0,2)$ has left side $H_0^{22}-\frac23(\nabla_0k)^2=\frac43k^1q_{\ell}$ and right side $-\frac12(\partial\eta)_{02}q_{\ell}=-\frac13k^1q_{\ell}$ (all $W_r^{22}$ vanish). Hence $k^1q_{\ell}=0$; the pair $(1,2)$ gives $k^0q_{\ell}=0$, and $k^2=\kappa_{\ell}=0$.

(c) Now $k=0$, $\nabla k=0$ and $\partial\eta=0$, so $W_0=W_1=0$, $W_2=B_W$ at the point. For $(q,p)=(0,1)$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1\}$ the $(\alpha,\beta)$-entry of \eqref{c0:eq:I1} reads $(\nabla_0\ell_1-\nabla_1\ell_0)B_W^{\alpha\beta}=-T^2_{01}B_W^{\alpha\beta}$, i.e.\ $-2q_{\ell}B_W^{\alpha\beta}=-q_{\ell}B_W^{\alpha\beta}$. The remaining entries of $B_W$ are $B_W^{a2}=k^a=0$.
<!-- end proof-86 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{c0:thm:qzero}
On $\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:qzero}
 q_\ell=A(\ell,\ell)=0,\qquad
 \kappa_\ell=B_W(\ell,\ell)=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-87: body_md -->
The open set $U_0:=\{q_{\ell}\ne0\}\cap\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}$ is independent of the choice of $\ell$. Suppose $U_0\ne\emptyset$. On $U_0$, Lemma~\ref{c0:lem:pureprol}(a) gives $\kappa_{\ell}\equiv0$, then (b) gives $k\equiv0$, then (c) gives $B_W\equiv0$; hence $W\equiv0$ and $\partial\eta=0$ on $U_0$. Lemma~\ref{c0:lem:mixed} then gives $\operatorname{Sym}[\overline{\Xi_{pl}}A^{aj}]=0$ on $U_0$, and contraction with $z_az_jz_l$ gives
\[
 \left(\sum_l\overline{\Xi_{pl}}z_l\right)
 \left(\sum_{a,j}A^{aj}z_az_j\right)=0.
\]
The quadratic factor is nonzero because $q_{\ell}\ne0$; cancellation in
$\mathbb C[z_0,z_1,z_2]$ gives $\Xi=0$. Thus $\mathcal P$ is totally
symmetric on $U_0$. At a point with $\ell=e^2$, $\mathcal P^{2,jl}=0$, so by total symmetry every component of $\mathcal P$ with an index $2$ vanishes. Total symmetry is preserved by $\nabla'$, so $\nabla_p\mathcal P=M_p\mathcal P$, and hence $A\mathsf J_p\mathcal P$, is totally symmetric. For $j,l\in\{0,1\}$ this gives $\sum_b(A\mathsf J_p)_{2b}\mathcal P^{b,jl}=(A\mathsf J_p\mathcal P)^{j,2l}=0$. For $p=0$ the left side is $A^{22}\varepsilon_{201}\mathcal P^{1,jl}=q_{\ell}\mathcal P^{1,jl}$, for $p=1$ it is $A^{22}\varepsilon_{210}\mathcal P^{0,jl}=-q_{\ell}\mathcal P^{0,jl}$. Thus $\mathcal P=0$ at the point, contradicting $\operatorname{rank}\mathcal P=2$. Hence $q_{\ell}\equiv0$ on $\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}$, and \eqref{c0:eq:qrec} gives $\ell_p\kappa_{\ell}\equiv0$, i.e.\ $\kappa_{\ell}\equiv0$.
<!-- end proof-87 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:rzero}
If $r=A\ell\equiv0$ on an open set $V\subset\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}$, then $k=B_W\ell\equiv0$, i.e.\ $\partial\eta\equiv0$, on $V$.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-88: body_md -->
By \eqref{c0:eq:elltr} and \eqref{c0:eq:Kform}, $\nabla_pr=(\nabla_pA)\ell+A\nabla_p\ell=\gamma_pr+W_p\ell+A\mathsf J_pr$, and $W_p\ell=\ell_pk-\frac13(e_p\kappa_{\ell}+\ell_pk)=\frac23\ell_pk$ since $\kappa_{\ell}=0$ (Theorem~\ref{c0:thm:qzero}). If $r\equiv0$ on $V$ this gives $\ell_pk=0$ for all $p$, so $k=0$.
<!-- end proof-88 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:ellbar}
On $\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}$:
\textup{(a)} $\psi=0$;
\textup{(b)} for every $\zeta\in \mathcal E^*$, $\ (k\cdot\zeta)\,\beta_\ell-(r\cdot\zeta)\,a_\ell\ \in\ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{ann}}\otimes K_X^{-1}$ (i.e.\ it is a $K_X^{-1}$-valued multiple of $\ell$).
Consequently, on the open set $U_\times:=\{x\in\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}:A\ell\wedge B_W\ell\ne0\}$,
$\beta_\ell\wedge\ell=a_\ell\wedge\ell=0$; in an adapted frame $\ell=e^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:uxinput}
 \beta_{\bar2}\bmod\ell=0,\qquad
 (\mathcal P^{\alpha,\beta\gamma})_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\{0,1\}}
 \text{ is totally symmetric}.
\end{equation} Where $B_W\ell=\varkappa\,A\ell\ne0$, $\varkappa\,\beta_\ell-a_\ell\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{ann}}$.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-89: body_md -->
Contract the identity of Lemma~\ref{c0:lem:mixed}, $\operatorname{Sym}_{(l,a,j)}\bigl[\nabla_{\bar l}W_p^{aj}-\overline{\Xi_{pl}}A^{aj}\bigr]=0$, with $\zeta_l\ell_a\ell_j$; with $D_\xi W_p(y,z):=\sum_l\xi_l(\nabla_{\bar l}W_p)(y,z)$ and $q_{\ell}=0$ this gives
\begin{equation}\label{c0:eq:mixedcontr}
 D_\zeta W_p(\ell,\ell)+2D_\ell W_p(\ell,\zeta)=2\,(a_\ell)_p\,(r\cdot\zeta).
\end{equation}
We evaluate the left side with \eqref{c0:eq:Kform}, $\kappa_{\ell}\equiv0$, $\nabla''\kappa_{\ell}=0$ (i.e.\ $G_l(\ell,\ell)=-2k\cdot\beta_{\bar l}$, $G_l:=\nabla_{\bar l}B_W$) and a local extension of $\zeta$ with $\nabla\zeta=0$ at the point. From $W_p(\ell,\ell)=\frac13\ell_p\kappa_{\ell}\equiv0$ and $W_p(v,\ell)=\ell_pB_W(v,\ell)-\frac13(v_p\kappa_{\ell}+(k\cdot v)\ell_p)=\frac23\ell_p(k\cdot v)$ we get $(\nabla_{\bar l}W_p)(\ell,\ell)=-2W_p(\beta_{\bar l},\ell)=-\frac43\ell_p\,k\cdot\beta_{\bar l}$, and
\[
 (\nabla_{\bar l}W_p)(\zeta,\ell)=\nabla_{\bar l}\bigl(W_p(\zeta,\ell)\bigr)-W_p(\zeta,\beta_{\bar l})
 =\beta_{\bar l,p}\,(k\cdot\zeta)+\ell_p\bigl(\tfrac23G_l(\ell,\zeta)-\tfrac13B_W(\zeta,\beta_{\bar l})\bigr)+\tfrac13\zeta_p\,k\cdot\beta_{\bar l}.
\]
Hence \eqref{c0:eq:mixedcontr} reads
\[
 -\tfrac43\ell_p\,k\cdot\beta_{\bar\zeta}+2(\beta_\ell)_p(k\cdot\zeta)+\tfrac23\zeta_p\psi+2\ell_p\bigl(\tfrac23G_\ell(\ell,\zeta)-\tfrac13B_W(\zeta,\beta_\ell)\bigr)=2(a_\ell)_p(r\cdot\zeta),
\]
with $\beta_{\bar\zeta}:=\sum\zeta_l\beta_{\bar l}$, $G_\ell:=\sum\ell_lG_l$. For $\zeta=\ell$ (using $k\cdot\ell=\kappa_{\ell}=0$, $r\cdot\ell=q_{\ell}=0$, $B_W(\ell,\beta_\ell)=\psi$ and $G_\ell(\ell,\ell)=-2\psi$) the left side is $\ell_p(-\frac43\psi+\frac23\psi-\frac83\psi-\frac23\psi)=-4\ell_p\psi$, and the right side is $0$; this is (a). Modulo $\ell$ and with $\psi=0$ the displayed identity is $2(k\cdot\zeta)\beta_\ell\equiv2(r\cdot\zeta)a_\ell$, which is (b). If $r\wedge k\ne0$ choose $\zeta$ with $r\cdot\zeta=0\ne k\cdot\zeta$ and then $\zeta$ with $k\cdot\zeta=0\ne r\cdot\zeta$. In an adapted frame $(a_\ell)_p=\overline{\Xi_{p2}}$ and $\Xi_{p2}=\mathcal P^{1,p0}-\mathcal P^{0,p1}$.
<!-- end proof-89 -->
<!-- lemma-44: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:Ux}
At every point of $U_\times$: \textup{(a)} $\mathsf T_2=0$ (the adjugate of $\bar A|_F$ is apolar to the cubic $\bar c$); \textup{(b)} $\mathsf M\beta^\perp_{\bar y}+\mathsf T_y=0$ for $y=0,1$; \textup{(c)} $r^1\beta^\perp_{\bar0}-r^0\beta^\perp_{\bar1}=-(Q_{20},Q_{21})$; hence \textup{(d)} $\mathsf M\,(Q_{20},Q_{21})^{\mathsf T}=r^1\mathsf T_0-r^0\mathsf T_1$.
<!-- end lemma-44 -->
<!-- proof-90: body_md -->
$\Phi_a:=a_\ell\wedge\ell$ and $\Phi_b:=\beta_\ell\wedge\ell$ vanish on $U_\times$. Differentiate $\Phi_a$ along $\bar y$ with $\nabla_{\bar y}\overline{\mathcal P}=\overline{M_y\mathcal P}$ and $\nabla_{\bar y}\ell=\beta_{\bar y}$: the transverse part is $\mathsf M\beta^\perp_{\bar y}+\mathsf T_y$ (the terms with $\beta_{\bar y,2}$ and $\eta$ drop by (b) of Proposition~\ref{c0:prop:ellbar}); for $y=2$ use $\beta^\perp_{\bar2}=0$. Differentiate $\Phi_b$ along $y$: by the Ricci identity $\nabla_y\beta_{\bar x}=\nabla_{\bar x}\nabla_y\ell+R_{y\bar x}\cdot\ell$ and \eqref{c0:eq:elltr}, modulo $\ell$ one gets $\bigl[\beta(\varepsilon_y(r))+\varepsilon_y((\nabla_{\bar\ell}A)\ell)-R_{y\bar\ell}\cdot\ell\bigr]\wedge\ell=0$ with $\beta(\zeta)=\sum\zeta_x\beta_{\bar x}$; The algebraic expansion in Step~1 of Appendix~\ref{calc:c0:thm:hol},
with $x=2$, gives
\[
 [\varepsilon_y((\nabla_{\bar2}A)\ell)-R_{y\bar2}\cdot\ell]_b
       =\delta_{y2}Q_{2b}\qquad(b=0,1).
\]
This uses only \eqref{c0:eq:barA} and \eqref{c0:eq:decomp}, not the
holomorphic-annihilator conclusion. For $y=0,1$, also
$\varepsilon_y(r)\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{ann}}$, so the preceding identity
is zero; for $y=2$ it gives (c). Part~(d) is (b) combined with (c).
<!-- end proof-90 -->
<!-- lemma-45: body_md -->
\label{c0:lem:rawmixed}
On any open subset of $\Omega_{\mathcal P,2}$ where $a_\ell\wedge\ell=0$, with the same adapted-frame definitions of $\mathsf M,\mathsf T$, one has
\[
 (\nabla_{\bar y}(a_\ell\wedge\ell))_{p2}
 =(\mathsf M\beta_{\bar y}^{\perp}+\mathsf T_y)_p=0,
 \qquad p=0,1,\quad y=0,1,2.
\]
No nonvanishing of $r$ and no vanishing of $\beta_{\bar2}^{\perp}$ is required.
<!-- end lemma-45 -->
<!-- proof-91: body_md -->
Differentiate the full tensor $a_\ell\wedge\ell$, using
$(a_\ell)_p=\sum_l\ell_l\overline{\Xi_{pl}}$,
$\nabla_{\bar y}\ell=\beta_{\bar y}$, and
$\nabla_{\bar y}\overline{\mathcal P}=\overline{M_y\mathcal P}$.
Only after the product rule specialize $\ell=e^2$, $q_{\ell}=0$ and $\ell\mathcal P=0$.
The terms involving transverse $\beta$ are exactly the displayed $2\times2$ matrix $\mathsf M$; the remaining terms are $\mathsf T_y$. Terms proportional to $\ell$ and the half-Lee term cancel because $a_\ell\wedge\ell=0$. This is the same fixed $(p,2)$ component expansion as in Lemma~\ref{c0:lem:Ux}; setting $y=2$ requires no extra assumption until one wishes to replace the resulting equation by $\mathsf T_2=0$.
<!-- end proof-91 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{c0:prop:Uxdich}
At every point of $U_\times$ exactly one of the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\lambda=\mu=0$; equivalently, in an adapted frame,
\begin{equation}\label{c0:alt0}
 \beta_{\bar x,a}=\vartheta'\delta_{xa}\quad(x,a=0,1),\qquad
 m_{00}=m_{11}=0,\quad m_{10}=-m_{01},
\end{equation}
where $m_{\alpha\beta}=\mathcal P^{\alpha,\beta2}$.
\item There are linear forms $s$ and $l\ne0$ on $F$ with
\begin{equation}\label{c0:alt1}
 A(z)=(r\cdot z')\,(s(z')+2z_2),\qquad
 B_W(z)=(k\cdot z')\,(s(z')+2z_2),
\end{equation}
$\lambda=(r\cdot z')l$ and $\mu=(k\cdot z')l$; the form $s$ may be zero. In particular $\operatorname{rank} A\le2$, $\operatorname{rank} B_W\le2$, and the quadrics $A$ and $B_W$ have a common linear factor.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-92: body_md -->
Comparing the coefficients of $z_2^1$ and $z_2^0$ in $\lambda B_W=\mu A$ gives $\lambda\,(k\cdot z')=\mu\,(r\cdot z')$ and $\lambda (B_W)_F=\mu A_F$. On $U_\times$ the linear forms $r\cdot z'$, $k\cdot z'$ are independent, so by unique factorization in $\mathbb C[z_0,z_1]$ either $\lambda=\mu=0$, or $\lambda=(r\cdot z')l$ and $\mu=(k\cdot z')l$ with the same $l\ne0$; in the latter case $(r\cdot z')(B_W)_F=(k\cdot z')A_F$ gives $A_F=(r\cdot z')s$ and $(B_W)_F=(k\cdot z')s$ with the same $s$.
